\onlineid\vgtccategory

Research pdftitle=ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming, pdfauthor=Haoran Liu, Di Wu, Wang Luo, Hengyuan Na, Miao Hu, and Guocong Quan \vgtcinsertpkg\hypersetup\teaserRepresentative full-scene volumetric video scenarios and our mobile playback.

Introduction

ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming

Haoran Liu Di Wu Wang Luo Hengyuan Na Miao Hu and Guocong Quan

Abstract

Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose , a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB over a controlled V-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.3ResStreamGS3

Mobile volumetric video streaming, real-time rendering, 3D Gaussian Splatting.

keywords

Volumetric video enables users to freely explore dynamic 3D scenes from arbitrary viewpoints and supports immersive applications such as virtual reality, mixed reality, and remote telepresence. Bringing these experiences to commodity mobile devices remains challenging because a practical system must maintain high visual quality while reducing transmission, decoding, memory, and rendering costs. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides a promising representation for this setting because its explicit point-based formulation supports high-quality reconstruction and efficient rasterization . To further reduce transmission and decoding costs, recent systems organize time-varying Gaussian attributes into 2D video-like representations and compress them more effectively with commodity hardware codecs such as H.264 and HEVC .[]16[, , ]412032

Existing Gaussian-video pipelines encode the complete Gaussian representation as a frame-varying signal. This design is effective for human-centric or foreground-dominant content, where many important primitives change together with the moving subject. Complex full-scene volumetric videos have a different temporal structure. Dynamic regions occupy only part of the scene, while large portions of the geometry and appearance remain persistent over time. Treating all Gaussians in such scenes as frame-varying signals may therefore introduce unnecessary processing and distortion.

To better understand this limitation, we conduct an empirical study by applying the same V-style H.264 Gaussian-video pipeline to both foreground-focused and complex full-scene content. As shown in fig:v3_quality_drop, Neu3D consistently exhibits a much steeper PSNR decline across increasing QP values than Actors-HQ; under the default setting, the drops are 11.7 dB and 3.4 dB, respectively. More importantly, the qualitative results in fig:qualitative_comparison show that the errors are not limited to rapidly moving regions. Scene structures that should remain largely stable can also become visibly corrupted. These results suggest that the all-Gaussians formulation is poorly matched to the temporal structure of complex full-scene content.3\cref\cref

These results further motivate us to examine why full-scene content suffers more degradation. Our analysis in Sec.  shows that the key issue lies in a mismatch between the temporal behavior of Gaussian primitives and the granularity at which they are processed. Existing pipelines repeatedly adapt and encode every primitive at the frame level, even though many primitives change little within a short frame group. As a result, stable primitives are exposed to optimization drift and codec distortion without providing benefits in temporal adaptability. This observation suggests that Gaussian primitives should not be uniformly processed at the same temporal granularity. Stable primitives can instead be reused across frames, while only primitives sensitive to temporal residuals need to remain in the frame-wise adaptation and video-coding path.3

Motivated by these findings, we propose , a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework for efficient full-scene volumetric video streaming. ResStreamGS first uses lightweight probe adaptation to identify primitives that are sensitive to temporal changes. It then selects the smallest residual-sensitive subset that preserves the reconstruction quality of the composed scene. The remaining primitives are treated as stable references and reuse their keyframe attributes within the Group of Pictures (GOP). This partition produces two synchronized streams with different temporal granularities. Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP and cached on the mobile device, while residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in a compact frame-wise Gaussian-video stream that can be decoded with commodity video hardware. In this way, ResStreamGS retains the advantages of hardware video decoding while removing persistent scene state from repeated frame-wise processing.ResStreamGS

Experiments on full-scene volumetric videos demonstrate that this design substantially improves both reconstruction fidelity and streaming efficiency. Under the same Gaussian-video coding framework, ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB over the controlled V all-Gaussians baseline while reducing the amortized payload by up to 56.5%. Our mobile implementation achieves 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G mobile platform, showing that high-quality full-scene volumetric video can be played in real time on commodity mobile hardware.3

(1) We identify a temporal mismatch in Gaussian-video streaming, where primitives with different temporal behaviors are uniformly processed at the frame level. This motivates processing Gaussians according to their temporal sensitivity. (2) We propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that separates stable Gaussians for GOP-level reuse from residual-sensitive Gaussians for frame-level adaptation, with quality-aware selection to preserve reconstruction quality. (3) ResStreamGS substantially improves post-codec reconstruction quality while reducing the amortized streaming payload by up to 56.5%, and consistently achieves 30.883 FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G mobile platform for smooth real-time full-scene volumetric video playback in practical mobile deployment scenarios.Our Contributions:New Perspective.Novel Framework.Superior Performance.

1

1.1

Dynamic novel view synthesis (NVS) reconstructs time-varying 3D scenes from videos for novel-view rendering. Early methods extend NeRF with deformation fields, scene flow, or time conditioning to model dynamic content . Later explicit and factorized representations improve efficiency using voxel grids, multi-plane decompositions, or tensorized 4D structures , but still rely on costly volumetric sampling or neural decoding.[, , , , , ]30353426399[, , , , ]7401836

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) instead adopts an explicit point-based representation with rasterization-oriented rendering . Dynamic 3DGS methods further model temporal changes through deformation fields, Gaussian tracking, frame-wise updates, or pose-dependent Gaussian maps . Although these methods achieve high reconstruction quality and rendering speed, their large per-frame storage and limited compatibility with commodity video codecs make direct deployment for mobile volumetric video streaming challenging .[]16[, , , , , , , ]4329251449505224[, , ]432924

1.2

Despite efficient rasterization, 3DGS introduces substantial storage overhead because each Gaussian stores geometry, opacity, and view-dependent appearance attributes . Existing compact 3DGS methods mainly reduce this cost through opacity- or contribution-aware pruning, vector quantization, entropy coding, codebook-based clustering, and context-adaptive prediction . These techniques show that Gaussian representations contain spatial and attribute redundancy and can be compressed without severely degrading rendering quality. However, they are designed for static scenes, where the representation is decoded once and reused across viewpoints. Dynamic Gaussian sequences further amplify the storage burden as geometry and appearance evolve over time. Recent methods therefore exploit temporal redundancy through keyframes, residual modeling, motion-aware updates, and memory-efficient 4D parameterizations . Streaming-oriented approaches employ adaptive layering and saliency-aware tiling to reduce transmission cost . Nevertheless, most methods optimize how the complete Gaussian sequence is compressed, without distinguishing primitives that remain stable over time. Our work instead separates stable Gaussians from residual-sensitive ones before dynamic encoding, avoiding repeated lossy compression of stable structures and reserving the dynamic stream for time-varying content.[]16[, , , , , ]1831336215[, , , ]1948346[, ]1110

1.3

Mobile volumetric video systems must jointly reduce network bandwidth, decoding overhead, and rendering cost on mobile devices. Early systems based on point clouds or meshes employ visibility-aware scheduling, adaptive transmission, view-dependent content selection, and edge-assisted processing to support interactive playback under constrained resources . Recent 3DGS systems extend these ideas by adapting transmitted content, quality, or bitrate according to network conditions and user viewpoints . SwinGS  further adopts a sliding-window design to limit memory consumption and support longer volumetric video sequences. Video-coded Gaussian streaming takes a complementary direction by exploiting commodity video hardware. V maps dynamic Gaussian attributes into 2D Gaussian videos, enabling H.264 compression, hardware decoding, and shader-based rendering on mobile devices. Vega  further improves full-scene mobile streaming through object-level selective computation and view-adaptive scheduling, while MobileGS and SEELE optimize client-side Gaussian processing and rasterization . Despite these advances, existing video-coded pipelines still treat all Gaussians as temporally varying signals and repeatedly pass them through frame-wise compression. This can unnecessarily expose stable background primitives to quantization noise and optimization-induced attribute drift. Our work instead isolates stable Gaussians before encoding, preserving them across frames while retaining compact dynamic streams for real-time mobile playback.[, , ]134712[, , , , , , ]45372711104438[]283[]41[]17[, ]551

2

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives . Each primitive is parameterized as[]16G={gi}i=1NG=\{g_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}

gi=(𝐩i,𝐪i,𝐬i,αi,𝐜i),g_{i}=\left(\mathbf{p}_{i},\mathbf{q}_{i},\mathbf{s}_{i},\alpha_{i},\mathbf{c}_{i}\right),(1)

with , , , , and describing its position, rotation, scale, opacity, and view-dependent color, respectively. The rotation and scale determine the spatial extent of a Gaussian through its covariance matrix. Under a viewing transformation , the covariance is projected onto the image plane as𝐩i\mathbf{p}_{i}𝐪i\mathbf{q}_{i}𝐬i\mathbf{s}_{i}αi\alpha_{i}𝐜i\mathbf{c}_{i}𝐖\mathbf{W}

𝚺i=𝐑i​𝐒i​𝐒iT​𝐑iT,𝚺i′=𝐉𝐖​𝚺i​𝐖T​𝐉T,\mathbf{\Sigma}_{i}=\mathbf{R}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}\mathbf{S}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{R}_{i}^{T},\qquad\mathbf{\Sigma}^{\prime}_{i}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{\Sigma}_{i}\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{J}^{T},(2)

in which and are the rotation and scaling matrices, is the Jacobian of the projective transformation, and gives the projected covariance. During rendering, the Gaussians overlapping a pixel are depth-sorted and accumulated through front-to-back alpha blending:𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i}𝐒i\mathbf{S}_{i}𝐉\mathbf{J}𝚺i′\mathbf{\Sigma}^{\prime}_{i}

𝐂=∑i∈𝒩𝐜i​αi′​∏j=1i−1(1−αj′),\mathbf{C}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}}\mathbf{c}_{i}\alpha^{\prime}_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha^{\prime}_{j}),(3)

where contains the ordered Gaussians contributing to the pixel and is the corresponding projected opacity. This explicit representation enables efficient rasterization while maintaining high-quality novel-view rendering. For dynamic scenes, a volumetric video can therefore be viewed as a temporal sequence of these Gaussian attributes, whose values evolve from frame to frame.𝒩\mathcal{N}αi′\alpha^{\prime}_{i}

Building on this explicit representation, V organizes dynamic 3DGS into frame groups for volumetric video streaming. The first frame of each group is reconstructed as a keyframe, and subsequent frames are optimized sequentially from the preceding Gaussian representation. Motion is first estimated for the Gaussian primitives, followed by fine-tuning of the remaining attributes to improve temporal consistency across frames. By maintaining a consistent set of primitives within each frame group, the attributes of the same Gaussian can be associated across consecutive frames rather than reconstructed independently at every time step. After training, the per-frame Gaussian attributes are packed into 2D attribute images for video coding. V applies Morton sorting before packing so that spatially neighboring Gaussians are placed at nearby image locations, improving the spatial coherence of the resulting attribute maps. The same ordering is retained across attribute images and consecutive frames, allowing corresponding pixel locations to represent the same Gaussian primitive over time. As a result, the evolution of Gaussian attributes is converted into temporally coherent image sequences that can be compressed using conventional video codecs such as H.264. On mobile devices, hardware video decoders recover the attribute maps for standard 3DGS rendering.3[]413

3

In this section, we investigate why existing all-Gaussians video coding is poorly suited to complex full-scene volumetric video. This leads to our first research question.

3.1

Existing Gaussian-video pipelines treat the complete Gaussian representation as a frame-varying signal, which is well suited to human-centric content where many important primitives change together with the moving subject. Full-scene sequences such as and , in contrast, contain localized dynamic regions together with large persistent backgrounds and room-scale structures . To examine whether the same coding paradigm remains effective under this different temporal structure, we apply the V-style H.264 pipeline to both foreground-focused Actors-HQ and full-scene Neu3D across different quantization settings. As shown in fig:v3_quality_drop, Neu3D exhibits substantially faster PSNR degradation as QP increases, whereas Actors-HQ remains comparatively stable. Under the default setting, the corresponding drops are 11.7 dB and 3.4 dB, respectively, making the degradation on full-scene content more than three times larger. This consistent gap indicates that all-Gaussians video coding is substantially less effective for complex full-scene content.Effectiveness Analysis.cook_spinachcoffee_martini[]233\cref

To understand where this degradation occurs, we further examine the reconstructed scenes after Gaussian-video coding. As shown in fig:qualitative_comparison, the errors are not limited to rapidly moving objects or regions with strong temporal changes. Scene structures that should remain largely stable can also become visibly corrupted. This suggests that the degradation cannot be explained only by the difficulty of representing dynamic content. Instead, the frame-wise pipeline may unnecessarily perturb scene content that could otherwise remain persistent.Error Analysis.\cref

All-Gaussians video coding is substantially less effective for complex full-scene content than for foreground-dominant content, with considerable degradation even in scene structures that should remain temporally stable.Finding of RQ1.

This finding raises our second research question.

3.2

To identify the source of this degradation, we analyze nominally stable regions in through successive stages of the reconstruction and coding pipeline. As shown in fig:intro_diagnostic(a), using the frozen Gaussians as the reference, frame-wise retraining alone introduces a 4.69 dB PSNR drop, while subsequent video coding causes another 1.74 dB drop, resulting in a total degradation of 6.43 dB. This decomposition shows that stable scene content is affected by both frame-wise optimization and lossy video coding rather than by codec distortion alone.Stage-Wise Analysis.cook_spinach\cref

The attribute-level analysis in fig:intro_diagnostic(b) further shows that frame-wise retraining perturbs multiple Gaussian attributes even for primitives whose underlying scene content changes little. These slightly changed attributes are then repeatedly quantized and reconstructed as temporal video signals, introducing additional distortion. This problem is particularly severe for full-scene content because a large portion of its Gaussians correspond to persistent geometry and appearance within a short GOP. Frame-wise processing provides little benefit for these primitives, yet the all-Gaussians pipeline still repeatedly adapts and encodes them. Importantly, temporal stability does not correspond directly to a semantic foreground-background partition: some spatially stationary primitives still require frame-dependent updates, while some primitives near dynamic regions remain sufficiently stable for reuse. The key distinction should therefore be whether each primitive is sensitive to temporal changes that affect reconstruction quality.Temporal Mismatch Analysis.\cref

The degradation arises from a mismatch between primitive-level temporal behavior and frame-level processing. Uniformly adapting and encoding all Gaussians unnecessarily exposes reusable stable primitives to both optimization drift and codec distortion during repeated frame-wise processing stages.Finding of RQ2.

Gaussian primitives should be processed according to their temporal sensitivity rather than uniformly at the frame level. Stable primitives can be represented once and reused within a GOP, while only residual-sensitive primitives need to remain in the frame-wise adaptation and video-coding path.Insight for ResStreamGS.

4

Motivated by the above insight, we propose , an end-to-end residual-sensitive dual-stream framework for efficient mobile 3DGS streaming, as illustrated in Fig. . ResStreamGS organizes Gaussians according to their temporal sensitivity into a group-level stable stream and a frame-level residual-sensitive stream. The framework consists of server-side dual-stream GOP processing and mobile-side composition and rendering.ResStreamGS4

On the server side, ResStreamGS initializes the Gaussian representation from the keyframe and performs lightweight GOP probing to profile multi-attribute residual sensitivity. It then ranks the primitives according to their sensitivity and applies quality-aware ratio selection to partition them into stable and residual-sensitive subsets. Stable Gaussians are retained at the GOP level and reused across its frames, while residual-sensitive Gaussians undergo frame-wise motion estimation and fine-tuning to capture temporal variations. After optimization, the two subsets are organized into different transmission forms: stable Gaussians are encoded as a stable packet transmitted once per GOP, whereas residual-sensitive Gaussians are arranged into a compact frame-wise Gaussian video compatible with hardware-supported codecs for efficient transmission.

On the mobile side, the stable packet is received once at the beginning of each GOP and cached in device memory for reuse across subsequent frames. In parallel, the residual-sensitive Gaussian video is decoded frame by frame using commodity hardware video decoding. For each frame, the decoded residual-sensitive Gaussians are combined with the cached stable Gaussians to reconstruct the complete Gaussian representation for the current scene state. Given the current user viewpoint, ResStreamGS further applies view-frustum culling to discard invisible primitives, followed by opacity-based pruning to remove Gaussians with negligible rendering contributions. The remaining Gaussians are then depth-sorted and rendered to produce the final view. In this way, the mobile client avoids repeatedly decoding and storing persistent scene content while retaining frame-wise updates for temporally sensitive regions.

For each frame group (GOP) , ResStreamGS takes the keyframe Gaussian set as its group-level reference. The keyframe establishes primitive correspondence and provides the initial values for all Gaussian attributes. The last frame of serves as the probe target. A lightweight probe temporarily adapts the keyframe representation to this target using the calibrated training views of the probe target frame. During adaptation, the probe records per-primitive attribute changes. 4.2

Selective optimization keeps fixed within the GOP and produces frame-dependent attributes for . The following subsection describes how the two representations are encoded as a reusable stable packet and a residual-sensitive Gaussian video.GsG^{s}GtrG^{r}_{t}

4.5

After optimization, encodes the stable set once per GOP for reuse and represents the frame-dependent residual-sensitive sets as a compact Gaussian video stream.ResStreamGSGsG^{s}GtrG^{r}_{t}

The attributes of remain fixed throughout the frame group . The stable packet is therefore encoded and transmitted once when the group is loaded. It stores the Gaussian attributes required for rendering together with the primitive indices needed to preserve their slots in the composed Gaussian set. The primitives are spatially ordered and packed by attribute type before entropy coding; the ordering, precision, and codec settings are reported in Sec. . retains the Gaussian video interface of V but applies frame-wise H.264/AVC coding only to , while remains outside the video path and is supplied by the reusable stable packet. We evaluate on six complex full-scene sequences from two multiview video datasets, including five from Neu3D  and one from MeetRoom . These sequences contain localized dynamic content together with substantial room-scale structures, matching the streaming setting considered in this work. Each sequence contains 300 consecutive frames and is divided into 20-frame GOPs.Datasets and Evaluation Protocol.ResStreamGS[]23[]22

For each Neu3D sequence, we reserve five calibrated camera views for held-out evaluation and use the remaining views for training. MeetRoom contains 11 calibrated views, of which 10 are used for training and one is reserved for held-out evaluation. Neu3D rendering is evaluated at resolution, while MeetRoom is evaluated at . The same frames, camera parameters, resolutions, GOP boundaries, training views, and held-out evaluation views are used for all locally evaluated methods. All rendering metrics are computed exclusively on held-out views across evaluated frames. Probe adaptation and quality-aware stream partitioning use only training views, and held-out views are not used for model optimization or stream-configuration selection. item.title: 开放式互动的双刃剑：LLM驱动的NPC如何影响玩家的认知负荷和游戏体验 ｜ The Double-Edged Sword of Open-Ended Interaction: How LLM-Driven NPCs Affect Players' Cognitive Load and Gaming Experience
item.description:
中文摘要：：本研究探讨了大型语言模型驱动的非玩家角色 (LLM-NPC) 如何影响玩家的认知负荷和游戏体验，特别关注潜在的心理机制、任务场景之间的差异以及个体特征的作用。我们在自主开发的游戏原型“校园文化周”中进行了随机受试者间实验（N=130），比较了玩家在多个交互模块中与LLM-NPC和传统预先编写的NPC的互动。结果表明，LLM-NPC 条件将自由形式的自然语言输入与 LLM 生成的响应相结合，比预设选项脚本化 NPC 产生更高的认知负荷

Conducting a randomized between-subject experiment (N=130) in a self-developed game prototype "Campus Culture Week", we com

[Submitted on 11 Apr 2026 (), last revised 18 Oct 2026 (this version, v3)]v1

Title:

, , , , Authors:Ting-Chen HsuWenran ChenJiangxu LinFei QinZheyuan ZhangView PDF
This study examines how large language model-driven non-player characters (LLM-NPCs) affect players' cognitive load and gaming experience, with a particular focus on the underlying psychological mechanisms, differences across task scenarios, and the role of individual traits. Conducting a randomized between-subject experiment (N=130) in a self-developed game prototype "Campus Culture Week", we compared player interactions with LLM-NPCs and traditional pre-scripted NPCs across multiple interactive modules. The results showed that the LLM-NPC condition, which combined free-form natural-language input with LLM-generated responses, produced higher cognitive load than preset-option scripted NPC interaction (p < .001), with expressive effort and response uncertainty as significant mediating pathways. However, LLM-NPCs did not yield a statistically significant improvement in overall gaming experience (p = .195); while they positively influenced players' perceived autonomy, they exerted a negative influence on system usability and trust. The effects of LLM-NPCs also significantly varied across task scenarios (p < .001), with stronger increases in cognitive load in more open-ended modules such as content creation and relationship building. The influence of individual differences was generally limited, with no robust associations remaining after correction for multiple comparisons. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding the "double-edged sword" effect of LLM-NPCs on player experience, and highlights the importance of scenario-sensitive and user-sensitive design in intelligent NPC systems. 15th October 2026

ToolLaTeX renderer— LaTeX renderer turns LaTeX source into a rendered view, either a single display equation typeset by MathJax or a full document or prose fragment typeset by faster-latex, with a live preview beside the editor and a toolbar switch between Edit and Rendered views. Source can be typed, loaded from a URL or GitHub Gist, or picked from built-in examples, and the page keeps the LaTeX in the URL fragment so it can be shared as a readable or compressed link.

Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

item.title: 皮克斯动画工作室将《Hoppers》的制作带到 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 ｜ Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of ‘Hoppers’ to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026
item.description:
中文摘要：通过| | , SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 年 10 月 15 日动画会议 图片来源：SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 提供的主要图片 今年 12 月，迪士尼和皮克斯《Hoppers》背后的创意团队将前往吉隆坡！

来源：SIGGRAPH Blog（English） 相关度：15.6 正文：2321 字 / 1 图

命中：siggraph

Go behind the scenes of Disney and Pixar’s "Hoppers" at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 as Pixar Animation Studios shares the creative decisions, technical innovations, and collaboration that brought the film to life. The post Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of ‘Hoppers’ to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 appeared first on ACM SIGGRAPH Blog .

Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of ‘Hoppers’ to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

by | | , SIGGRAPH Asia15 October 2026AnimationConferences

Image credit: Leading image provided by SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

This December, the creative minds behind Disney and Pixar’s “Hoppers” are heading to Kuala Lumpur!

SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 is excited to welcome Pixar Animation Studios for a Featured Speakers session, “We’re All In This Together: The Making Of Disney and Pixar’s ‘Hoppers,’” offering a behind-the-scenes look at the artistry, technology, and collaboration that brought the film to life.

Creating the world of “Hoppers” came with a unique challenge: Bringing together three distinct visual styles, from the graphic clarity of comedy and the carefully controlled lighting and staging of suspense to the rich, observational beauty of nature photography.

To bring these elements together, the filmmakers developed a collaborative approach that balanced stylization with realism, combining physical simulation and artistic design to create the film’s distinctive visual world.

At SIGGRAPH Asia 2026, the Pixar team will share insights into the creative decisions, technical innovations, and collaborative processes behind the film, highlighting how artists and technologists across different disciplines worked together to bring their vision to the screen.

Meet the Pixar Team at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

Layout lead, Pixar Animation Studios VFX supervisor, Pixar Animation Studios Tailoring and simulation supervisor, Pixar Animation StudiosAndrea Goh,Beth Albright,Lyon Liew,

More Exciting Program Highlights to Come!

And that’s not all! More exciting sessions, industry-leading speakers, and program highlights are still to be announced as we count down to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026.

Stay tuned to the as we continue to unveil what’s in store this December!SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 website

item.title: 基于色场的粒子分类，用于固体 SPH 模拟中的残余应力检测和减少 ｜ Colour-Field Based Particle Categorization for Residual Stress Detection and Reduction in Solid SPH Simulations
item.description:
中文摘要：：即使没有外力或热压力，物体中也会残留残余应力，从而可能导致显着的塑性变形。如果残余应力对材料产生不良影响，因此是不希望的，则需要有效的解决方案来跟踪和消除该应力。平滑粒子流体动力学已广泛应用于固体力学模拟，其固有的色场生成方法是一种很有前途的残余应力跟踪器。在本文中，我们提出了一种使用色场方法来消除残余应力并防止固体物体发生不良过早失效的方法。

来源：arXiv·cs.GR 分类（English） 相关度：15.4 正文：3444 字 / 3 图

命中：particle

arXiv:2610.24210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Residual stress remains in an object even in the absence of external forces or thermal pressure, which, in turn, may cause significant plastic deformations. In case the residual stress creates unwanted effects on the material and so is undesirable, an efficient solution is necessary to track and eliminate this stress. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics

[Submitted on 16 Oct 2026]

Title:

Authors:Gizem KayarView PDF
Residual stress remains in an object even in the absence of external forces or thermal pressure, which, in turn, may cause significant plastic deformations. In case the residual stress creates unwanted effects on the material and so is undesirable, an efficient solution is necessary to track and eliminate this stress. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics has been extensively used in solid mechanics simulations and the inherent colour-field generation approach is a promising tracker for the residual stress. In this paper, we propose a way to use the colour-field approach for eliminating the residual stress and prevent the undesirable premature failure of solid objects. Abstract:

item.title: 超越 UV 映射：通过表面对齐纹理字段进行网格纹理压缩 ｜ Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields
item.description:
中文摘要：：网格纹理压缩通常依赖于 2D UV 图集，其图表不连续性和映射开销会限制编码效率。为了应对这一挑战，我们引入了 TexF，一种表面对齐的纹理场，用于组织源自网格表面的稀疏体素中的纹理属性。这种表示支持高分辨率纹理，同时保留本地 3D 相关性以进行压缩并支持直接表面查询。对于比特流压缩，TexF 重用已建立的 3D 属性编解码器，从解码的网格重建体素位置，无需单独传输。对于 GPU 驻留压缩，我们开发了 3DNTC，它将量化哈希特征与 l

来源：arXiv·实时渲染（English） 相关度：15.4 正文：35254 字 / 6 图

命中：mesh、texture、rendering

Mesh texture compression typically relies on 2D UV atlases, whose chart discontinuities and mapping overhead can limit coding efficiency. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TexF, a surface-aligned texture field that organizes texture attributes in sparse voxels derived from the mesh surface. This representation supports high-resolution textures while preserving local 3D correlations for compre

Beyond UV Mapping: Mesh Texture Compression via Surface-Aligned Texture Fields

Jianqiang Wang Junhui Hou Siyu Ren Weiyao Lin Wenping Wang †This work was supported in part by the Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 62422118, and in part by the Hong Kong Research Grants Council under Grants 11220426, 11219324, and N_CityU1114/25.†thanks: †J. Wang, J. Hou, and S. Ren are with the Department of Computer Science, City University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China (Email: wang.jq@cityu.edu.hk; jh.hou@cityu.edu.hk; siyuren2-c@my.cityu.edu.hk)†thanks: †W. Lin is with the Department of Electrical Engineering, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China (e-mail: wylin@sjtu.edu.cn)†thanks: †W. Wang is with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Texas A&M University, TX 77840, US (Email: wenping@tamu.edu).†thanks:

Abstract

Mesh texture compression typically relies on 2D UV atlases, whose chart discontinuities and mapping overhead can limit coding efficiency. To tackle this challenge, we introduce TexF, a surface-aligned texture field that organizes texture attributes in sparse voxels derived from the mesh surface. This representation supports high-resolution textures while preserving local 3D correlations for compression and enabling direct surface queries. For bitstream compression, TexF reuses established 3D attribute codecs, with voxel locations reconstructed from the decoded mesh without separate transmission. For GPU-resident compression, we develop 3DNTC, which combines quantized hash features with a lightweight decoder for random-access reconstruction at surface positions. Differentiable rendering enables image-space refinement of both voxel attributes and compressed neural fields. Experiments on the MPEG and AOM mesh compression benchmarks demonstrate improved average rate–distortion performance over representative UV-based methods for both bitstream and GPU-resident compression. 3DNTC also supports real-time rendering. The code will be publicly available at .https://github.com/yydlmzyz1/TexF

3D Mesh, Texture Representation, Compression, Inverse Rendering.

Index Terms:

I Introduction

Textured 3D meshes are widely used to represent 3D assets, enabling the depiction of continuous geometric surfaces with high-fidelity visual appearances. With the rapid expansion of immersive media and spatial intelligence , the efficient representation and compression of these assets have become essential . While the geometric surface provides the structural foundation, the texture component is a key factor in visual realism and often constitutes a major portion of the overall bitrate. Texture compression is challenging not only because of its data volume, but also because texture must remain aligned with the underlying surface and preserve rendered visual quality.[]1[]2[, ]34

Existing mesh compression pipelines typically store geometry as polygonal meshes and appearance in separate 2D texture atlases through UV parameterization , as illustrated on the left of Fig. . Within this paradigm, mature image/video codecs such as HEVC  and AV1  produce compact bitstreams for storage and transmission. Hardware-supported texture formats such as ASTC  and neural texture compression (NTC) methods  reduce GPU-resident memory while supporting random access during rendering. Despite their different coding mechanisms, these methods share the same 2D UV atlas representation. However, UV atlas construction can separate nearby surface regions into disjoint charts, weakening the spatial correlations exploitable by 2D codecs, while also introducing padding, packing, and UV-mapping overhead. Both effects can reduce coding efficiency, particularly for meshes with complex geometry. These limitations motivate alternative ways to organize texture for compression.[, , ]5671[, ]89[, ]104[]11[]12

Beyond compression, texture representation has long been explored outside the UV domain, primarily for appearance modeling, authoring, and rendering. UV-free methods associate texture with mesh elements or locations in 3D space. Related representations include mesh-attached textures , volumetric textures , and neural or implicit textures . Some of these efforts also address texture storage through sparse octrees , compressed 3D blocks , or voxel serialization . Yet these storage reductions do not necessarily translate into better compression than established UV-based pipelines. Inefficient modeling of spatial correlations and additional indexing overhead can offset the savings from removing UV mappings, and even increase storage. These considerations suggest that effective mesh texture compression requires jointly addressing texture organization and mapping overhead. We therefore investigate how mesh surface geometry can guide texture organization and coding in 3D, beyond simply removing UV mappings.[, ]1314[, , ]151617[, ]1819[, ]1620[]21[]22

Our central idea is to use the mesh surface itself to determine where texture attributes are stored and how they are accessed. We introduce , a that stores texture attributes only in voxels intersected by the mesh surface (right of Fig. ). This surface-aligned organization offers three advantages for compact representation and compression. First, surface-localized sparsity supports high-resolution, high-fidelity textures without a dense volume, using sample counts comparable to those of 2D texture maps. Second, texture locations can be derived from the mesh, reducing the storage overhead of separate surface-to-texture mappings and spatial indices. Third, organizing texture attributes directly in 3D preserves their native spatial relationships for compression, avoiding the disruption of spatial coherence caused by UV charting or reordering.TexFsurface-aligned texture field1

We construct TexF through direct texture transfer from a UV-textured mesh. We develop an efficient, differentiable renderer that queries texture attributes directly at mesh surface positions. The renderer also enables inverse-rendering (IR) refinement , using multi-view image-space supervision to reduce transfer and discretization errors.[, , , ]23242526

We exploit TexF’s surface-aligned structure for both bitstream and GPU-resident texture compression. For bitstream compression, we encode voxel attributes directly using established 3D attribute codecs, including Unicorn  and G-PCC , exploiting spatial correlations in their native 3D neighborhoods. Voxel locations are reconstructed from the decoded mesh, avoiding separate voxel-position coding and UV-mapping overhead. For GPU-resident compression, we develop a neural codec that captures 3D spatial correlations in quantized multiresolution hash features. A compact decoder reconstructs attributes on demand at surface positions, supporting random access during rendering .[]27[]28[, ]2912

Experiments on the standard MPEG  and AOM  benchmarks demonstrate that TexF with Unicorn significantly outperforms the evaluated UV-based pipelines in averaged rate–distortion performance, including those enhanced by UV reparameterization and alternative image codecs. Competitive results with G-PCC further show that these benefits are not confined to a single coding backend. For GPU-resident compression, TexF generally achieves better rate–distortion performance than conventional and neural UV texture compression, while supporting random-access decoding during rendering.[]30[]4

In summary, we present a mesh texture compression framework based on a surface-aligned texture field (TexF). Specifically:

  • •

    TexF stores and accesses texture in a sparse 3D field aligned with the underlying mesh surface, enabling compact, high-resolution, and UV-free representation. An efficient differentiable renderer supports direct surface queries and inverse-rendering refinement.

  • •

    We exploit TexF’s native 3D spatial correlations for both bitstream and GPU-resident compression. Bitstream compression reuses established 3D attribute codecs without separately transmitting voxel locations. GPU-resident compression uses quantized hash features and a lightweight decoder for random-access surface queries without explicit per-voxel lookup entries.

  • •

    We systematically compare TexF with UV-based and serialization-based alternatives, demonstrating improved average rate–distortion performance in both compression settings and analyzing how asset characteristics affect the relative performance of TexF and UV representations.

    • The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. comprehensively reviews existing work on the representation of mesh texture and its compression. Sec. presents the proposed method, followed by extensive experiments and a series of promising future directions in Sec. . Finally, Sec. concludes this workIIIIIIVV

    II Related Work

    Compression of a textured mesh involves both geometry and texture. Geometry coding represents vertex positions and connectivity using methods such as Draco ; comprehensive reviews are provided in . Our focus, instead, is mesh texture compression.[]6[, ]531

    Since the texture representation determines the signal exposed to subsequent coding, we organize prior work according to how texture is associated with the mesh surface, broadly distinguishing UV-based and UV-free approaches. UV atlases remain the prevailing representation in production pipelines, underlying both texture bitstreams for storage and transmission and GPU-resident payloads for rendering. Fig.  summarizes the representations, their construction, and the associated compression methods. Here, it is worth noting that describes how texture is associated with the mesh surface, rather than the domain in which the resulting signal is compressed.2UV-free

    II-AUV-based Mesh Textures

    A UV-textured mesh associates its surface with coordinates in a 2D texture domain. Surface parameterization partitions the mesh into charts and unfolds them onto the plane. Parameterization methods seek to limit angular or area distortion , while atlas packing arranges the resulting charts in a UV atlas with gutters to improve image utilization and reduce filtering artifacts . When constructing a new atlas, texture baking resamples the source appearance into the new UV layout. The resulting regular 2D images are compatible with mature image/video coding tools and GPU texture formats.UV parameterization and atlas construction.[, ]3233[]34

    For storage and transmission, UV-based texture can be encoded using established codecs such as H.265/HEVC  and AV1 . MPEG V-DMC  organizes mesh textures into video-compatible representations and reuses established video coding tools. Reparameterization  and atlas packing can improve texture coding efficiency, but may incur substantial preprocessing cost for complex meshes.Bitstream-oriented compression.[]8[]10[, ]79[]34

    For runtime GPU memory, block-based image formats derived from block truncation coding , including S3TC  and ASTC , provide fixed-rate storage and hardware-supported random access. Random-access neural texture compression (NTC)  instead represents material using quantized latent grids and a compact decoder, enabling on-demand reconstruction from a GPU-resident representation at the cost of per-material optimization.GPU-resident compression.[]35[]36[]11[]12

    Despite the practical advantages of UV-based pipelines, chart-based unfolding changes the native surface neighborhoods exposed in the atlas: regions adjacent on the mesh may fall into different charts, weakening correlations across chart boundaries. Chart packing also introduces padding, while the explicit surface-to-atlas mapping requires UV coordinates and associated indices. Constructing a new atlas also incurs preprocessing cost, and texture resampling can introduce distortion before compression. Careful parameterization and packing mitigate these costs but do not remove the dependence on chart layout, motivating complementary representations that preserve appearance directly in 3D space.Limitations of the UV domain.

    II-BUV-free Mesh Textures

    UV-free texture representations associate appearance directly with mesh elements or locations in the surrounding 3D space, avoiding dependence on a global UV atlas. This long-standing idea has inspired diverse approaches to appearance modeling, authoring, and rendering, whereas its application to mesh texture compression remains comparatively limited.

    1 II-B

    UV-free texture representations differ primarily in how they associate appearance with the mesh surface.

    A separate family attaches appearance directly to mesh elements. Per-vertex colors provide the simplest example, although their spatial resolution is limited by the vertex density of the mesh. Per-face methods such as Ptex  assign an independent 2D texture to each face and maintain a per-face adjacency map for cross-face filtering. Mesh Colors  and Patch Textures  associate color samples with mesh elements without explicit UV coordinates. However, their global organization follows mesh connectivity rather than a single regular lattice, complicating the direct reuse of mature image- or volume-based codecs. These systems primarily address parameterization-free authoring and rendering rather than texture compression.Mesh-attached textures.[]13[]14[]37

    Volumetric texture representations associate appearance directly with positions in 3D space. Early solid textures  define appearance procedurally as a function of 3D position and are particularly suited to materials with volumetric patterns, such as wood or stone. Shell Maps  instead construct a surface-aligned volumetric parameterization by mapping a tetrahedral shell around the mesh into texture space. Octree-based textures  instead organize sampled surface attributes in adaptive octree hierarchies for parameterization-free painting and rendering. TexF instead defines a surface-aligned texture field directly in the mesh coordinate system, with voxel locations derived from the mesh rather than stored in a separate hierarchy.Volumetric textures.[, ]1538[]17[, , ]163920

    In recent years, neural methods have represented appearance using continuous coordinate functions or learned features. Oechsle et al.’s neural Texture Fields  represent appearance as a continuous function conditioned on shape features, avoiding explicit surface parameterization. NeuMesh  instead attaches learned geometry and texture features to mesh vertices for neural rendering and editing. In contrast, NeuTex  learns a continuous mapping from 3D surface points to a 2D neural texture domain. These neural texture methods primarily target appearance modeling, reconstruction, or editing. TexF instead starts from explicit texture attributes on mesh-derived voxels, providing a common representation for both 3D attribute codecs and GPU-resident neural compression.Neural and implicit textures.[]18fθ​(x,y,z)→RGBf_{\theta}(x,y,z)\rightarrow\mathrm{RGB}[]40[]19

    2 II-B

    UV-free representations have been widely studied for appearance modeling, authoring, and rendering, but comparatively few works address mesh texture compression. These works differ in how they organize surface attributes for coding.

    As an early effort, CB3TM  retains surface-relevant regions of a solid texture and applies 3D Haar-wavelet coding with coefficient truncation to local subvolumes for independent reconstruction. Although not mesh-specific, the 3D mode of ASTC  provides fixed-rate coding of regular 3D blocks. Both exploit local 3D correlations and support random access, but their dense coding units limit the use of fine-grained surface sparsity.[]21434^{3}[]11

    Dolonius et al.  used octree-derived Sparse Voxel Directed Acyclic Graphs (SVDAGs) to compactly represent voxelized surfaces and address separately stored attributes. The attributes are linearized along Morton or Hilbert curves, then compressed with a custom random-access codec or mapped to 2D for existing image and GPU texture codecs. These methods exploit spatial coherence through the serialized ordering. While SVDAG-based methods use a separate voxel hierarchy for texture access, TexF uses the mesh surface as the common spatial basis for representation, compression, and rendering. This surface-aligned organization supports native 3D attribute coding and direct neural queries at surface positions.[, ]2241

    II-CRelated 3D Coding and Optimization Techniques

    Beyond mesh-texture representations, research on 3D coding and differentiable rendering provides tools that TexF draws on for construction and compression.

    Broader volumetric-data research has developed compression methods for regular and sparse 3D signals . These techniques generally target volume data or voxel scenes rather than appearance associated with a separate triangle mesh. Point cloud codecs provide related tools for attributes defined on known 3D support, but do not themselves define a mesh-texture representation or renderer. V-PCC projects point cloud patches into packed 2D images, whereas G-PCC operates on geometry and attributes in the 3D point set . Learned point cloud attribute codecs, such as Unicorn , further explore data-driven spatial transforms and entropy models . TexF makes these codecs applicable to mesh textures by organizing attributes on mesh-derived voxels, whose positions can be reconstructed from the decoded mesh without separate transmission.3D spatial coding.[, , , ]11424344[, ]4528[]27[, ]4647

    Multiresolution hash encoding  maps spatial coordinates to trainable features stored in compact hash tables. We adapt this encoding to GPU-resident TexF compression, using quantized features and lightweight decoding inspired by NTC . By replacing explicit voxel attributes with a directly queryable compressed field, the codec avoids storing per-voxel lookup entries.Multiresolution hash encoding.[]29[]12

    Inverse rendering optimizes geometry or appearance by propagating image-space supervision through a differentiable rendering process . TexF uses this supervision both to reduce transfer and discretization errors during representation construction and to refine the compressed neural field.Inverse rendering.[, , , ]23242526

    III Proposed Method

    Conventional mesh texture compression operates on 2D UV atlases. We instead organize texture attributes in a (), whose sparse voxel support is derived from the mesh surface. Thus surface positions can directly query the 3D field, providing a common spatial basis for texture representation, compression, and rendering.surface-aligned texture fieldTexF

    As illustrated in Fig. , we construct TexF by voxelizing the mesh surface and transferring the source texture, then refine its attributes through differentiable rendering to reduce transfer and discretization errors. Based on this representation, we develop two complementary schemes: bitstream compression with established 3D attribute codecs for disk storage and transmission, and GPU-resident neural compression for memory-efficient random access during rendering.3

    III-ASurface-aligned TexF Representation and Construction

    TexF associates texture attributes with voxels derived from the mesh surface, preserving spatial locality without UV parameterization. We efficiently construct this support through surface voxelization and initialize its attributes from the source texture.

    1 III-A

    Given a textured mesh , we first discretize its canonical axis-aligned bounding box into a grid. TexF and the mesh geometry therefore share a common coordinate system, allowing surface points to query the field directly in 3D space without an intermediate parameterization such as UV mapping. The surface-aligned TexF retains only voxels intersecting the mesh surface, referred to as active voxels. Their indices form the active set , with and . In practice, we construct this sparse support efficiently through surface sampling and voxelization without allocating the dense grid. This surface-localized sparsity supports high-resolution texture representation with sample counts comparable to those of 2D texture maps, avoiding the high memory cost of dense volumetric textures. Each voxel in the active set stores texture attributes , defining TexF as𝐌\mathbf{M}K×K×KK\times K\times K𝐐\mathbf{Q}𝐪∈ℤ3\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}0≤𝐪<K0\leq\mathbf{q}<KK3K^{3}𝐪\mathbf{q}𝐐\mathbf{Q}𝐭⁡(𝐪)\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{q})

    𝒯={(𝐪,𝐭⁡(𝐪))∣𝐪∈𝐐},\mathcal{T}=\{(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{q}))\mid\mathbf{q}\in\mathbf{Q}\},(1)

    where encodes base color (i.e., RGB) by default and can be extended channel-wise to include other physically-based rendering (PBR) material attributes, such as roughness and metallicity.𝐭⁡(𝐪)\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{q})

    A textured mesh is thus represented by its geometry and the associated TexF , forming a mesh with TexF. Surface positions query texture directly in their shared 3D coordinate system, without UV coordinates or a separate surface parameterization. Because the voxel support is derived from the mesh and grid configuration, its coordinates need not be separately transmitted. This organization preserves local 3D spatial relationships among texture attributes, supporting direct surface queries and spatially coherent attribute coding, as described in Secs.  and .𝐌\mathbf{M}𝒯\mathcal{T}III-BIII-C

    TexF’s spatial structure also offers representational versatility. It naturally shares a voxel grid with grid-based implicit geometry, such as an SDF, for joint geometry–appearance modeling. Its attributes can also be sampled at mesh vertices for vertex-color rendering. Examples are provided in the .Remark.Supplementary Material

    2 III-A

    To support conventional UV-textured assets, we initialize TexF by sampling the mesh surface and transferring attributes from the source texture. For each surface sample, its barycentric coordinates determine both its 3D position and UV coordinate. The UV coordinate is used to sample the source material maps, while the 3D position assigns the retrieved attributes to the corresponding voxel. Attributes assigned to the same voxel are averaged. Conversely, TexF can be baked into a UV texture by rasterizing a target UV layout and querying the field at the corresponding surface positions, enabling compatibility with standard UV rendering pipelines. Voxel discretization and interpolation introduce transfer errors, which we reduce through rendering-driven refinement in Sec. .III-B

    III-BTexF Rendering and Refinement

    1 III-B

    TexF rendering first rasterizes the mesh to determine visible surface positions, then queries the field at these positions to obtain texture attributes. As illustrated in Fig. , UV rendering samples a 2D texture through interpolated UV coordinates, whereas TexF queries the field directly at . For the voxel representation defined in Eq. (), the color is obtained by trilinearly interpolating neighboring texture attributes:4𝐩\mathbf{p}1𝐜⁡(𝐩)\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p})

    𝐜⁡(𝐩)=∑i∈𝒩⁡(𝐩)ωi​𝐭​(𝐪i),\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p})=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p})}\omega_{i}\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{q}_{i}),\vskip-4.26773pt(2)

    where denotes the set of active grid points within the neighborhood of , and the trilinear weights are determined by the query position within the grid cell. This interpolation is mathematically analogous to bilinear sampling in UV rendering, but operates in 3D with weights renormalized over the available voxels. In the rare case that no active corner is available, the nearest active voxel is used as a fallback. We implement this rendering path using differentiable rasterization  and sparse-grid interpolation operators . The interpolation in Eq. () is differentiable and can be evaluated in parallel, supporting real-time rendering and efficient backpropagation to the voxel attributes. GPU-resident TexF uses the same rasterization stage, but interpolates latent features and decodes them with an MLP to obtain texture attributes (Sec. ).𝒩⁡(𝐩)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p})2×2×22\times 2\times 2𝐩\mathbf{p}ωi\omega_{i}[]48[]492III-D

    2 III-B

    We use our differentiable renderer to refine texture appearance through inverse rendering. We render reference images from the original lossless UV-textured mesh and corresponding images from the target mesh with TexF under the same views. We minimize the photometric objective{𝐈i}i=1N\{\mathbf{I}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}{𝐈^i}i=1N\{\widehat{\mathbf{I}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}

    𝒟=∑i=1N[‖𝐈^i−𝐈i‖1+1−SSIM⁡(𝐈^i,𝐈i)],\mathcal{D}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\left\|\widehat{\mathbf{I}}_{i}-\mathbf{I}_{i}\right\|_{1}+1-\mathrm{SSIM}(\widehat{\mathbf{I}}_{i},\mathbf{I}_{i})\right],\vskip-2.84544pt(3)

    where the term measures pixel-wise color errors and the SSIM term encourages structural similarity. Starting from the transferred attributes, we optimize while keeping the mesh geometry and voxel support fixed.ℓ1\ell_{1}𝐭⁡(𝐪)\mathbf{t}(\mathbf{q})

    Image-space supervision accounts for the sampling and interpolation used during rendering, allowing refinement to compensate for errors left by direct texture transfer and voxel discretization. It therefore improves the texture representation without increasing its capacity. This refinement is also efficient, requiring only a modest optimization cost in our experiments. The same objective also optimizes the latent features and decoder parameters of the compressed neural field (Sec. ).III-D

    Beyond compression refinement, the differentiable renderer could support mesh texturing directly from multi-view images. Extending it to jointly optimize geometry and appearance is another direction for future work.

    III-CTexF Bitstream Compression

    For disk storage and transmission, we seek a compact entropy-coded texture bitstream . TexF derives voxel locations from the mesh rather than encoding them separately. As illustrated in Fig. , mesh geometry is encoded using an existing mesh codec . The encoder and decoder apply the same voxelization procedure to the reconstructed mesh to obtain the voxel set . These shared locations establish the correspondence between decoded attributes and TexF voxels, allowing the texture stream to carry coded attributes without per-voxel coordinates.[, ]345[, , ]5316𝐐\mathbf{Q}

    To encode the attributes, we leverage established 3D coding tools. Just like UV-based pipelines use image or video codecs such as HEVC  and AV1 , TexF interfaces with point cloud attribute codecs through its compatible coordinate–attribute structure. Their transform, prediction, and entropy-coding tools can therefore exploit spatial correlations directly in mesh-derived voxel neighborhoods, without requiring a texture-specific codec architecture.[]8[]10

    The interface is : compatible 3D attribute codecs can be used without changing the TexF representation. We use Unicorn  as the primary backend, leveraging its multiscale neural transform and conditional entropy model. We also evaluate conventional RAHT -based attribute coding in G-PCC  to examine whether TexF’s compression gains extend across different coding architectures. Beyond these two backends, the same interface allows TexF to benefit from advances in compatible 3D attribute codecs without changing the representation. At the decoder, reconstructed attributes are restored to their corresponding voxel locations, recovering .codec-agnostic[]27[]50[]28𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}}

    III-DGPU-Resident TexF Compression

    GPU-resident compression aims to reduce texture memory while supporting low-latency random access during rendering . Although TexF is spatially sparse, its explicit attributes and lookup structure can still occupy substantial GPU memory at high resolutions. For example, our uncompressed implementation stores three 8-bit RGB values and a 64-bit lookup key per voxel. We therefore develop 3D Neural Texture Compression (), which exploits TexF’s 3D-native organization to compress surface appearance into quantized features and a lightweight decoder. Unlike NTC , which decodes texture attributes in the 2D UV domain, 3DNTC reconstructs them directly at continuous mesh surface positions, without UV mapping or explicit per-voxel lookup entries.[]123DNTC[]12

    1 III-D

    3DNTC uses two spatially downsampled hash grids with INT4 features to capture texture variations at different spatial scales, together with a shared four-layer FP16 MLP (Fig. ). At level , the grid resolution is , where is the reference spatial resolution set according to the source texture resolution, and is the downsampling factor (e.g., 4 or 8). Following multiresolution hash encoding , each level uses a table of entries with feature channels, indexed by hashing integer grid coordinates. These entries store shared latent features, without explicit per-voxel lookup keys. Thus, the downsampling factor controls spatial granularity, while and determine latent storage; varying these parameters adjusts the rate–distortion trade-off.6i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}⌈K/si⌉\lceil K/s_{i}\rceilKKsis_{i}[]292hi2^{h_{i}}FFsis_{i}hih_{i}FF

    2 III-D

    Rasterization provides visible surface positions as in Sec. . For each position , we hash the eight surrounding grid-corner coordinates at each level and trilinearly interpolate their features. The interpolated features are concatenated across levels into and combined with an 18-dimensional positional encoding . A single evaluation of the decoder then reconstructs color:III-B𝐩\mathbf{p}Φ⁡(𝐩)∈ℝ2​F\Phi(\mathbf{p})\in\mathbb{R}^{2F}γ⁡(𝐩)\gamma(\mathbf{p})D𝜽D_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}

    𝐭^​(𝐩)=D𝜽​(Φ⁡(𝐩),γ⁡(𝐩)),\widehat{\mathbf{t}}(\mathbf{p})=D_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\!\left(\Phi(\mathbf{p}),\gamma(\mathbf{p})\right),(4)

    Interpolating features before decoding yields the attribute directly at , avoiding separate neural decoding of the eight voxel-corner colors. The decoder has three hidden layers with 64, 48, and 32 channels and hardGELU activations, followed by a linear output layer; its parameters are shared across all surface queries within each asset. Only the packed latent tables and decoder parameters need to remain resident as texture data. Queries are independent and require no sequential entropy decoding, enabling on-demand reconstruction during rendering.𝐩\mathbf{p}

    3 III-D

    For each asset, we sample continuous surface positions and obtain target attributes from the refined explicit TexF. We jointly optimize the latent tables and MLP to minimize attribute mean squared error, simulating INT4 quantization during training. We then refine both against ground-truth multi-view renderings using Eq. (), improving rendered fidelity without increasing the payload. At deployment, only the packed latent tables and decoder parameters are needed as GPU-resident texture data. Detailed settings are provided in the .3Supplementary Material

    IV Experiments

    In this section, we first present the common experimental settings and assess TexF’s representation fidelity, compactness, and rendering efficiency. We then compare its bitstream and GPU-resident compression performance with UV-based and other alternatives, followed by ablation studies and further analysis.

    IV-AExperimental Settings

    1 IV-A

    To evaluate performance across diverse geometries and textures, we use eight human models from the MPEG mesh compression benchmark  and 32 assets from the AOMedia mesh coding test set . The AOM assets include scanned objects, plants and animals, DCC-created assets, and architectural models. Together, the two benchmarks comprise 40 assets with texture resolutions ranging from 2K to 4K. Detailed asset statistics and the complete test sets are provided in the , and representative assets are shown in Fig. .[]30[]41 We use 1K, 2K, and 4K to denote resolutions of 1024, 2048, and 4096, respectively.11Supplementary Material7

    2 IV-A

    To isolate texture-coding efficiency, all methods use the same geometry and evaluation protocol. Following the common test conditions  and MPEG official metrics, we assess quality using renderings from 16 fixed orthographic views distributed on a Fibonacci sphere at resolution, evaluated using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS  metrics, complemented by point-sampled 3D-PSNR following the standard evaluation procedure. The 16 fixed orthographic evaluation views are held out from rendering-driven optimization, which instead uses independently sampled perspective views.[]30222https://github.com/MPEGGroup/mpeg-pcc-mmetric[]512048×20482048\times 2048[]52

    We compare only the texture-related payload, since . Rate is measured as bitstream size (KB) or GPU-resident memory (MB). We quantify relative bitrate savings using BD-BR  and provide detailed R–D curves. Detailed payload accounting is provided in the corresponding sections. Computational efficiency is evaluated by runtime. We use an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB) with Intel Xeon Silver 4309Y CPUs for runtime measurements.all methods use the same geometry[]53
