and is optimized jointly with the photometric loss of the splatting model.ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}

3.5

In our pipeline, the ray tracer is not used as a replacement renderer. It serves as a sparse visibility oracle for evaluating transmittance along sampled light directions.

The 3DGS rasterizer is a highly optimized, tile-based renderer: for each screen-space tile it collects all projected splats overlapping the tile, sorts them in front-to-back order, and evaluates color and opacity via elliptical weighted average (EWA) splatting in that order. This design delivers excellent throughput for primary views but is tied to camera projection and ordered blending per tile.[]43

A point-based ray tracer allows us to evaluate Gaussian splatting from any point in space in any direction. The 3D starting points for our rays are computed from the expected-depth map . Following 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT) , each 3D Gaussian is enclosed by an anisotropically stretched regular icosahedron and the triangles of this proxy mesh are inserted into a BVH for fast ray-triangle traversal. The proxy is scaled so that it tightly bounds the region where the particle’s response exceeds a small minimum . The scale explicitly incorporates the particle’s opacity so that nearly transparent splats receive proportionally tighter bounds (”adaptive clamping”), which reduces false-positive hits during traversal. Rays then query the BVH to gather the next batch of intersections, evaluate contributions in sorted order, and early-terminate once the accumulated transmittance reaches a preset threshold.zEz_{E}[]26ϵ\epsilonα\alpha

For occlusion-only queries, we use the fact that transmittance along a ray can be accumulated multiplicatively where is the per-hit attenuation computed from the Gaussian’s line integral along the ray segment covered by the proxy. Because multiplication commutes, the hits need not be depth-sorted for this visibility pass. They can be processed in arbitrary order while maintaining correctness for . We early-terminate when . In practice, should match the early-out used by the rasterizer to keep consistency between visibility estimated by ray tracing and the screen-space renderer. To make the ray tracer a drop-in companion to standard 3DGS (so we can reuse pretrained point clouds and the existing rasterizer), we evaluate Gaussians on a ray with the same EWA-splatting formulation as the rasterizer. For a ray , we instantiate a one-pixel virtual camera at whose optical axis is (i.e., a local camera frame aligned with the ray). We then reuse the unmodified rasterizer to splat exactly the Gaussians reported by the BVH for that ray into the center pixel of this virtual camera. This yields consistent blending with the original tile-based renderer while allowing us to drive the evaluation from rays rather than from a full image plane.T←T⋅(1−Δai)T\leftarrow T\cdot(1-\Delta_{a_{i}})Δai\Delta_{a_{i}}TTT≤Ts​t​o​pT\leq T_{stop}Ts​t​o​pT_{stop}r⁡(t)=o+t​dr(t)=o+tdoodd

Alternative ray-based renderers make different evaluation choices that deviate from EWA splatting: 3DGRT evaluates each Gaussian at the maximum response along the ray and processes batches of intersections in sorted order using a k-buffer scheme. IRGS collapses 3D Gaussians to planar 2D Gaussian disks to obtain a closed-form ray-splat intersection. These choices are effective but generally require training with their respective renderer to avoid a mismatch with classic 3DGS splatting.[]26[]15[]16

3.6

Our optimization method consists of a two-stage strategy, as shown in Fig. .2

The first step in our optimization pipeline is pretraining a standard Gaussian model with the extension that we jointly train the normal . During this stage, we observe partially transparent regions where background color can leak through the object silhouette. To address this, we add an opacity-mask lossInitial stage.n^\hat{n}

ℒm​a​s​k=‖α^−M‖1,\mathcal{L}_{mask}=||\hat{\alpha}-M||_{1},(10)

where is the rendered opacity and is the binary foreground mask. By measuring the deviation of Gaussian splats from the expected surface, we find that this term reduces that deviation and pulls splats closer to the surface, yielding a better-defined geometry proxy for our ray-tracing pass.α^\hat{\alpha}MM

We use the color reconstruction loss from standard Gaussian splatting, the normal loss , and the opacity-mask loss . The full loss function for our initial stage is:ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n}ℒm​a​s​k\mathcal{L}_{mask}

ℒi​n​i​t=ℒc+ℒn+λm​a​s​k​ℒm​a​s​k.\mathcal{L}_{init}=\mathcal{L}_{c}+\mathcal{L}_{n}+\lambda_{mask}\mathcal{L}_{mask}.(11)

After pretraining the 3D Gaussian model, we freeze geometric Gaussian attributes (positions, covariance, opacity, and normals) and optimize BRDF material parameters jointly with the HDR environment map. We use an L1 photometric loss with unit weight in this stage. For reproducibility, Tab.  enumerates trainable/frozen variables and active losses for both stages.Second stage.ℒ1p​b​r\mathcal{L}^{pbr}_{1}1

Implementation-specific optimization and runtime settings are summarized in the implementation details paragraph below.

The visibility ray tracer is implemented with NVIDIA OptiX, and our Gaussian-splatting training and relighting pipeline is built on top of the Gaussian-splatting Python framework . We pretrain for 30,000 iterations in stage 1 and 400 iterations in stage 2. On an NVIDIA RTX A6000 graphics processing unit (GPU), stage 1 takes around 15 minutes and stage 2 around 10 minutes. We observe that longer second-stage training degrades relighting quality because the albedo begins to absorb illumination information. We use a compact environment map and normal-based hemisphere sampling, which halves the number of rays per pixel compared with full-sphere sampling. With a environment map, there are 512 candidate directions, after hemisphere culling and empty-space removal, the OptiX visibility pass takes approximately 436 ms at the evaluation resolution, corresponding to about 127 MRays/s. This measures only transmittance-weighted visibility queries. A full second-stage optimization iteration takes approximately 1.25 s/it, while final PBR relighting renders at about 0.83 s/image. Forward relighting spends about 55% of its time on visibility queries and 44% on BRDF/environment-map integration.Implementation details.GSplat[]3616×3216\times 3216×3216\times 32

4

We compare our method against previous state-of-the-art methods and also present an ablation study to isolate the contribution of each design component. Baselines are selected based on popularity and code availability.

Our evaluation focuses on masked single-object scenes. This choice narrows the range of real-world inverse-rendering ambiguities (e.g., clutter, contact shadows, interreflections, and segmentation errors), but it is technically motivated by our lighting model: we sample illumination from a distant environment map, and without modeling secondary bounces the incident radiance can vanish when the environment is occluded by surrounding structures. Isolated objects therefore provide a well-defined direct-lighting signal and allow us to isolate the effect of explicit visibility queries.

4.1

We report experimental results on the synthetic TensoIR dataset for IR of single objects. It contains four objects, each with reference images rendered under ten different lighting conditions, along with albedo and normal maps. We evaluate normal-estimation quality using mean angular error (MAE). For relighting, NVS, and albedo reconstruction, we report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) . Some results of our method for each model can be seen in Fig. .[]18[]405

Following prior work, we compensate for the inherent albedo-shading scale ambiguity by scaling each predicted albedo with a single global RGB factor that minimizes MSE to the ground truth . We do not apply color correction , all reported and visualized synthetic albedo results therefore use this scale normalization unless stated otherwise. To visualize the HDR environment maps, we follow TensoIR  and apply gamma tonemapping to convert HDR radiance to low-dynamic-range (LDR) values for display. NVS results are rendered using PBR with the estimated material parameters and environment lighting.[, , , , , , ]2014118223014[]5[]18

4.2

We compare our method with previous inverse rendering methods, NeRFactor , InvRender , NVDiffrec , GS-IR , TensoIR and IRGS on the TensoIR synthetic dataset. All comparisons are performed using multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Tab. summarizes the quantitative comparison and Fig. shows a visual comparison.[]41[]42[]28[]22[]18[]1523

Our method is competitive with prior 3DGS-based IR approaches and improves over several earlier baselines across NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting. However, IRGS achieves the best overall results on this benchmark. These results position VisibilitySplat as a direct explicit-visibility baseline that remains competitive with specialized 3DGS-based IR methods while retaining the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline for training and visualization. We attribute our performance gains over earlier baselines primarily to the explicit visibility term: on masked, single-object scenes the dominant ambiguity is often cast-shadow visibility and mutual occlusion under direct environment lighting, while multi-bounce transport is comparatively weak. In this regime, sparse but physically grounded transmittance queries already provide a large part of the benefit for disentangling albedo and lighting. Compared to IRGS, our lightweight separation between rasterized splatting for efficient training/preview and sparse ray-based visibility queries offers a favorable practicality-accuracy trade-off, but still leaves room for improvement in terms of absolute reconstruction quality.[]15

Our main source of error is imperfect surface reconstruction rather than instability of the occlusion ray tracer. In particular, inaccurate normals lead to visibly curved shadow boundaries and local relighting artifacts (see Fig. ). This interpretation is consistent with our higher mean angular error compared to competing methods. Despite these geometric limitations, our relighting quality in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS remains competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.4(b)

At the measured evaluation resolution on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, final PBR relighting takes about 0.83 s/image, so the current implementation is not real-time. Forward relighting time is dominated by explicit visibility queries (about 55%) and discrete BRDF/environment-map integration (about 44%), the remaining time is spent on standard 3D Gaussian splatting and minor overhead. Thus, real-time deployment would require optimizing both the visibility pass and the PBR integration.800×800800\times 800

4.3

We conduct an ablation study on the components of our method to validate their effectiveness. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS for NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting on the Lego model from the TensoIR Synthetic dataset (Tab. ), including a PBR-only baseline without visibility and without opacity-mask loss, as well as single-component removals.3

We disable both the visibility ray tracer and the opacity-mask loss and optimize with PBR supervision alone. Interestingly, this baseline yields the highest NVS PSNR (and lowest LPIPS), though not the highest SSIM. We attribute this behavior to stronger appearance fitting, where albedo absorbs more illumination information and therefore reproduces the training lighting more easily. However, this entanglement hurts decomposition: albedo reconstruction and relighting quality both degrade compared to the full model.PBR-only baseline.

To isolate the visibility term, we compare the variant (with opacity-mask loss retained) against the full model. Reintroducing explicit visibility improves relighting metrics and yields cleaner shadow behavior, indicating better separation of material and illumination.Visibility.without visibility

As described in the optimization section, this term mainly acts through improved geometric support for ray-based visibility queries. Comparing with the full model shows lower relighting quality. Removing the opacity-mask loss also decreases albedo PSNR, while albedo SSIM and LPIPS remain nearly unchanged. This suggests that coarse albedo structure is preserved but radiometric consistency degrades. Better-defined occluding geometry from opacity regularization allows visibility rays to produce cleaner shadow estimates, which in turn stabilizes relighting.Opacity mask loss.without opacity loss

5

We present VisibilitySplat, an IR approach that augments 3DGS with a sparse visibility oracle for transmittance-weighted occlusion. Implemented using BVH-accelerated point-based ray tracing, the oracle complements the standard rasterized 3DGS training and visualization loop while injecting explicit visibility cues for material-illumination disentanglement. On a synthetic benchmark, we improve over several baselines in PSNR for NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting, while remaining competitive in SSIM and LPIPS. Ablations suggest that explicit visibility queries primarily improve relighting and decomposition quality, even when a PBR-only variant can score higher on NVS appearance metrics.

Our evaluation targets single, masked, static objects, behavior in cluttered or dynamic scenes, or under imperfect segmentation, is not assessed. The illumination model accounts for direct lighting only. Indirect transport (interreflection, subsurface, participating media) and very high-frequency environment lighting are not modeled. Finally, experiments are restricted to synthetic data, robustness to real captures, complex materials (e.g., glass, hair, translucency), and sensor noise remains untested.Limitations.

Future extensions include multi-object and full-scene evaluation, incorporation of indirect lighting, tighter coupling between splatting and visibility (e.g., differentiable or cached variants), improved geometric robustness, and investigations toward real-time deployment and comprehensive testing on real datasets.Future work.

We will release the full implementation and supporting resources upon publication of this paper.Code availability.

中文摘要：：我们通过引入用于重新照明以及材质和灯光分解的显式可见性模型来解决使用 3D 高斯泼溅 (3DGS) 的逆渲染问题。我们的方法通过稀疏可见性预言机增强了标准光栅化 3DGS 管道，该预言机可根据采样的照明方向估计高斯基元的透射率加权遮挡。该预言机使用由包围体层次结构 (BVH) 加速的基于点的光线追踪器来实现，并在逆渲染目标内进行稀疏查询，同时保留原始 3DGS 循环以提高训练效率、交互式可视化和工具兼容性。着色遵循基于物理的渲染

来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：13.2 正文：31835 字 / 16 图

命中：gaussian splatting、gaussian、splatting、lighting、occlusion、relight

VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting

Sven KlugeUniversity of RostockAlbert-Einstein-Straße 2218059 Rostock, Germanysven.kluge@uni-rostock.deOliver StaadtUniversity of RostockAlbert-Einstein-Straße 2218059 Rostock, Germanyoliver.staadt@uni-rostock.de

ABSTRACT

We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) and queried sparsely within the inverse-rendering objectives, while the original 3DGS loop is retained for training efficiency, interactive visualization, and tooling compatibility. Shading follows a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation with a principled microfacet bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) and low-resolution high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps. We evaluate our method on the TensoIR synthetic dataset against baselines based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), tensor representations, and 3DGS. The results show competitive performance and improvements over several earlier baselines for novel-view synthesis (NVS), albedo reconstruction, and relighting. Ablations indicate that explicit visibility modeling is an important contributor to relighting and material-illumination disentanglement, while pure PBR supervision can favor appearance fitting in NVS. Overall, the findings suggest that sparse, point-based visibility queries effectively complement rasterized splatting for inverse rendering while preserving the practical advantages of the 3DGS ecosystem.

Keywords

inverse rendering; 3D Gaussian splatting; relighting; visibility; physically based rendering

1

Inverse rendering (IR) seeks to recover geometry, reflectance, and illumination from images by inverting the image formation process. Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) enable high-fidelity novel-view synthesis (NVS) and have been extended toward relightable decompositions under unknown illumination (e.g., NeRFactor and TensoIR ), but their implicit volumetric formulation is costly to train and render. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) instead optimizes explicit point primitives via differentiable rasterization, enabling real-time rendering and practical tooling, and has recently been adopted for IR (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering (GS-IR) and Gaussian Inverse Rendering (GIR) ). A key challenge is visibility: screen-space alpha compositing provides limited information about cast shadows and mutual occlusion, which are crucial for stabilizing material-light disentanglement under unknown illumination. While 3DGS-based IR pipelines benefit from fast forward rendering, visibility signals derived from the rasterizer alone can be too weak or too view-dependent to constrain shadows robustly. Recent work, including Inter-Reflective Gaussian Splatting (IRGS), therefore augments splatting with ray-based visibility estimation . We take a pragmatic step along this trajectory by adding a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion from sampled lighting directions, while retaining the original 3DGS rasterization loop for training efficiency and interactive visualization. This lightweight division of labor injects physically meaningful visibility constraints without replacing the splatting renderer (Fig. ). Rather than proposing a highly specialized approximation or learned visibility model, we deliberately study a direct formulation based on explicit visibility queries. This provides a reference baseline for assessing how much transmittance-weighted visibility contributes to IR and relighting with 3DGS. Our contributions are as follows: (i) a sparse visibility oracle for 3DGS that estimates how much light reaches each Gaussian from sampled environment directions, implemented with a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH); (ii) a reference baseline on the TensoIR synthetic benchmark, including comparisons to NeRF-based, tensor-based, and 3DGS-based IR methods and ablations that isolate the effect of explicit visibility.[]25[]41[]18[]19[]22[]30[, ]14151

2

2.1

The original NeRF method introduced neural volumetric representations for NVS, with subsequent work improving anti-aliasing and efficiency via scale-aware integration and more explicit encodings . 3DGS further shifts computation to explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives rendered by a custom rasterizer, enabling real-time performance. Geometry-oriented variants and BVH-based Gaussian ray tracing broaden the representation toward editing and secondary-ray effects.[]25[, , , , , , ]2342713127[]19[, ]1637[]26

2.2

IR aims to recover geometry, materials, and illumination from images and is intrinsically ill-posed. Early NeRF-based methods reduced ambiguity with simplifying assumptions: PhySG represents bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (BRDFs) and lighting using spherical Gaussians (SGs) but omits complex visibility and indirect transport. NeRFactor factorizes shape and reflectance under unknown lighting. InvRender derives spatially varying indirect illumination directly from the learned radiance field to improve albedo recovery. Ref-NeRF improves specular handling via a reflected-radiance parameterization that also yields better normals. To raise physical fidelity without losing efficiency, TensoIR builds on tensor-factorized fields to support on-the-fly visibility queries and second-bounce effects during reconstruction. Complementary surface-aligned fields stabilize geometry and normals for IR pipelines . More recent work targets illumination modeling itself: ENVIDR learns a neural environment for shiny scenes. NeRF-as-Emitter replaces the distant-light assumption with a near-field light NeRF, improving accuracy under spatially varying illumination, and NeILF++ jointly learns incident-light and outgoing-radiance fields with inter-reflections to better disentangle material and lighting.Neural fields for inverse rendering:[]39[]41[]42[]31[]18[, ]3532[]21[]23[]38

Adopting 3DGS for IR leverages real-time forward rendering but introduces new challenges: splats lack native surface normals, and forward splatting does not natively model occlusion or multi-bounce light. GS-IR addresses these by regularizing per-Gaussian normals and baking visibility for secondary effects while recovering geometry, spatially varying bidirectional reflectance distribution functions (SVBRDFs), and environment lighting under unknown illumination. Subsequent work deepens physical correctness: GaussianShader estimates robust normals and per-splat shading for reflective scenes. DeferredGS decouples geometry from lighting and performs deferred shading for editable relighting and Ref-Gaussian targets glossy reflections with a specialized deferred pipeline. Beyond perfect mirrors, SSS-GS introduces subsurface scattering to a 3DGS framework using an explicit surface plus an implicit scattering component. To improve general relighting, RNG conditions radiance on view and light directions with shadow cues and depth refinement, while BiGS unifies surface and volumetric materials via bidirectional spherical harmonics (SH), supporting near- and distant-light setups. Finally, GI-GS explicitly decomposes direct/indirect components and uses lightweight path tracing on a G-buffer for multi-bounce global illumination, bringing 3DGS-based IR closer to physically faithful relighting at interactive rates. These efforts are complementary to geometry-focused 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) and surface extraction with Gaussian Opacity Fields (GOF) , as well as to BVH-accelerated Gaussian ray tracing for secondary-ray phenomena .Gaussian splatting for inverse rendering:[]22[]17[]33[]34[]10[]11[]24[]8[]16[]37[]26

We follow a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation similar to recent IR systems such as TensoIR , NeRFactor , and GS-IR . Image formation is expressed by the surface rendering equation with geometric visibility and an energy-conserving microfacet BRDF, while geometry, reflectance, and illumination are represented by differentiable fields and optimized from multi-view images. In practice, illumination is computed by evaluating the integral over scene lights and/or an environment map together with the visibility term . Many IR systems employ this same BRDF formulation but differ in how geometry, visibility, and indirect effects are estimated. For example, TensoIR introduces efficient online visibility and secondary shading, NeRFactor learns a visibility field, and GS-IR attaches BRDF parameters to Gaussians with an occlusion approximation.VV

3.3

Accurate recovery of incident illumination is essential for robust IR. We model distant lighting as a high-dynamic-range (HDR) spherical environment map parameterized in equirectangular coordinates . Unlike SGs or mixtures of SGs, this image-based representation preserves high-frequency angular detail and thus supports sharp cast shadows without requiring many analytic lobes.[]9

Each HDR environment-map texel stores radiance , and we optimize these values directly during training with solid-angle compensation to account for the non-uniform texel area of equirectangular maps.LL

Because reflectance acts as an angular low-pass filter, the recoverable illumination bandwidth is limited by the object’s BRDF lobes . Accordingly, we use a compact environment-map parameterization, with concrete settings summarized in the implementation details paragraph.[]29

3.4

Reconstructing scene geometry, in particular surface normals, is essential for IR and PBR.

We evaluate alternative depth formulations, including inverse-depth variants, and find that expected depth provides the best overall reconstruction quality and the most stable downstream supervision in our setting. 3.5

In our pipeline, the ray tracer is not used as a replacement renderer. It serves as a sparse visibility oracle for evaluating transmittance along sampled light directions.

The 3DGS rasterizer is a highly optimized, tile-based renderer: for each screen-space tile it collects all projected splats overlapping the tile, sorts them in front-to-back order, and evaluates color and opacity via elliptical weighted average (EWA) splatting in that order. This design delivers excellent throughput for primary views but is tied to camera projection and ordered blending per tile.[]43

A point-based ray tracer allows us to evaluate Gaussian splatting from any point in space in any direction. The 3D starting points for our rays are computed from the expected-depth map . Following 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT) , each 3D Gaussian is enclosed by an anisotropically stretched regular icosahedron and the triangles of this proxy mesh are inserted into a BVH for fast ray-triangle traversal. The proxy is scaled so that it tightly bounds the region where the particle’s response exceeds a small minimum . The scale explicitly incorporates the particle’s opacity so that nearly transparent splats receive proportionally tighter bounds (”adaptive clamping”), which reduces false-positive hits during traversal. Rays then query the BVH to gather the next batch of intersections, evaluate contributions in sorted order, and early-terminate once the accumulated transmittance reaches a preset threshold.zEz_{E}[]26ϵ\epsilonα\alpha

For occlusion-only queries, we use the fact that transmittance along a ray can be accumulated multiplicatively where is the per-hit attenuation computed from the Gaussian’s line integral along the ray segment covered by the proxy. Because multiplication commutes, the hits need not be depth-sorted for this visibility pass. They can be processed in arbitrary order while maintaining correctness for . We early-terminate when . In practice, should match the early-out used by the rasterizer to keep consistency between visibility estimated by ray tracing and the screen-space renderer. To make the ray tracer a drop-in companion to standard 3DGS (so we can reuse pretrained point clouds and the existing rasterizer), we evaluate Gaussians on a ray with the same EWA-splatting formulation as the rasterizer. For a ray , we instantiate a one-pixel virtual camera at whose optical axis is (i.e., a local camera frame aligned with the ray). We then reuse the unmodified rasterizer to splat exactly the Gaussians reported by the BVH for that ray into the center pixel of this virtual camera. This yields consistent blending with the original tile-based renderer while allowing us to drive the evaluation from rays rather than from a full image plane.T←T⋅(1−Δai)T\leftarrow T\cdot(1-\Delta_{a_{i}})Δai\Delta_{a_{i}}TTT≤Ts​t​o​pT\leq T_{stop}Ts​t​o​pT_{stop}r⁡(t)=o+t​dr(t)=o+tdoodd

Alternative ray-based renderers make different evaluation choices that deviate from EWA splatting: 3DGRT evaluates each Gaussian at the maximum response along the ray and processes batches of intersections in sorted order using a k-buffer scheme. IRGS collapses 3D Gaussians to planar 2D Gaussian disks to obtain a closed-form ray-splat intersection. These choices are effective but generally require training with their respective renderer to avoid a mismatch with classic 3DGS splatting.[]26[]15[]16

3.6

Our optimization method consists of a two-stage strategy, as shown in Fig. .2

The first step in our optimization pipeline is pretraining a standard Gaussian model with the extension that we jointly train the normal . During this stage, we observe partially transparent regions where background color can leak through the object silhouette. To address this, we add an opacity-mask lossInitial stage.n^\hat{n}

ℒm​a​s​k=‖α^−M‖1,\mathcal{L}_{mask}=||\hat{\alpha}-M||_{1},(10)

where is the rendered opacity and is the binary foreground mask. By measuring the deviation of Gaussian splats from the expected surface, we find that this term reduces that deviation and pulls splats closer to the surface, yielding a better-defined geometry proxy for our ray-tracing pass.α^\hat{\alpha}MM

We use the color reconstruction loss from standard Gaussian splatting, the normal loss , and the opacity-mask loss . The full loss function for our initial stage is:ℒc\mathcal{L}_{c}ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n}ℒm​a​s​k\mathcal{L}_{mask}

ℒi​n​i​t=ℒc+ℒn+λm​a​s​k​ℒm​a​s​k.\mathcal{L}_{init}=\mathcal{L}_{c}+\mathcal{L}_{n}+\lambda_{mask}\mathcal{L}_{mask}.(11)

After pretraining the 3D Gaussian model, we freeze geometric Gaussian attributes (positions, covariance, opacity, and normals) and optimize BRDF material parameters jointly with the HDR environment map. We use an L1 photometric loss with unit weight in this stage. For reproducibility, Tab.  enumerates trainable/frozen variables and active losses for both stages.Second stage.ℒ1p​b​r\mathcal{L}^{pbr}_{1}1

Implementation-specific optimization and runtime settings are summarized in the implementation details paragraph below.

The visibility ray tracer is implemented with NVIDIA OptiX, and our Gaussian-splatting training and relighting pipeline is built on top of the Gaussian-splatting Python framework . We pretrain for 30,000 iterations in stage 1 and 400 iterations in stage 2. On an NVIDIA RTX A6000 graphics processing unit (GPU), stage 1 takes around 15 minutes and stage 2 around 10 minutes. We observe that longer second-stage training degrades relighting quality because the albedo begins to absorb illumination information. We use a compact environment map and normal-based hemisphere sampling, which halves the number of rays per pixel compared with full-sphere sampling. With a environment map, there are 512 candidate directions, after hemisphere culling and empty-space removal, the OptiX visibility pass takes approximately 436 ms at the evaluation resolution, corresponding to about 127 MRays/s. This measures only transmittance-weighted visibility queries. A full second-stage optimization iteration takes approximately 1.25 s/it, while final PBR relighting renders at about 0.83 s/image. Forward relighting spends about 55% of its time on visibility queries and 44% on BRDF/environment-map integration.Implementation details.GSplat[]3616×3216\times 3216×3216\times 32

4

We compare our method against previous state-of-the-art methods and also present an ablation study to isolate the contribution of each design component. Baselines are selected based on popularity and code availability.

Our evaluation focuses on masked single-object scenes. This choice narrows the range of real-world inverse-rendering ambiguities (e.g., clutter, contact shadows, interreflections, and segmentation errors), but it is technically motivated by our lighting model: we sample illumination from a distant environment map, and without modeling secondary bounces the incident radiance can vanish when the environment is occluded by surrounding structures. Isolated objects therefore provide a well-defined direct-lighting signal and allow us to isolate the effect of explicit visibility queries.

4.1

We report experimental results on the synthetic TensoIR dataset for IR of single objects. It contains four objects, each with reference images rendered under ten different lighting conditions, along with albedo and normal maps. We evaluate normal-estimation quality using mean angular error (MAE). For relighting, NVS, and albedo reconstruction, we report peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index (SSIM), and learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) . Some results of our method for each model can be seen in Fig. .[]18[]405

Following prior work, we compensate for the inherent albedo-shading scale ambiguity by scaling each predicted albedo with a single global RGB factor that minimizes MSE to the ground truth . We do not apply color correction , all reported and visualized synthetic albedo results therefore use this scale normalization unless stated otherwise. To visualize the HDR environment maps, we follow TensoIR  and apply gamma tonemapping to convert HDR radiance to low-dynamic-range (LDR) values for display. NVS results are rendered using PBR with the estimated material parameters and environment lighting.[, , , , , , ]2014118223014[]5[]18

4.2

We compare our method with previous inverse rendering methods, NeRFactor , InvRender , NVDiffrec , GS-IR , TensoIR and IRGS on the TensoIR synthetic dataset. All comparisons are performed using multi-view images captured under unknown lighting conditions. Tab. summarizes the quantitative comparison and Fig. shows a visual comparison.[]41[]42[]28[]22[]18[]1523

Our method is competitive with prior 3DGS-based IR approaches and improves over several earlier baselines across NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting. However, IRGS achieves the best overall results on this benchmark. These results position VisibilitySplat as a direct explicit-visibility baseline that remains competitive with specialized 3DGS-based IR methods while retaining the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline for training and visualization. We attribute our performance gains over earlier baselines primarily to the explicit visibility term: on masked, single-object scenes the dominant ambiguity is often cast-shadow visibility and mutual occlusion under direct environment lighting, while multi-bounce transport is comparatively weak. In this regime, sparse but physically grounded transmittance queries already provide a large part of the benefit for disentangling albedo and lighting. Compared to IRGS, our lightweight separation between rasterized splatting for efficient training/preview and sparse ray-based visibility queries offers a favorable practicality-accuracy trade-off, but still leaves room for improvement in terms of absolute reconstruction quality.[]15

Our main source of error is imperfect surface reconstruction rather than instability of the occlusion ray tracer. In particular, inaccurate normals lead to visibly curved shadow boundaries and local relighting artifacts (see Fig. ). This interpretation is consistent with our higher mean angular error compared to competing methods. Despite these geometric limitations, our relighting quality in PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS remains competitive with state-of-the-art approaches.4(b)

At the measured evaluation resolution on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, final PBR relighting takes about 0.83 s/image, so the current implementation is not real-time. Forward relighting time is dominated by explicit visibility queries (about 55%) and discrete BRDF/environment-map integration (about 44%), the remaining time is spent on standard 3D Gaussian splatting and minor overhead. Thus, real-time deployment would require optimizing both the visibility pass and the PBR integration.800×800800\times 800

4.3

We conduct an ablation study on the components of our method to validate their effectiveness. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS for NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting on the Lego model from the TensoIR Synthetic dataset (Tab. ), including a PBR-only baseline without visibility and without opacity-mask loss, as well as single-component removals.3

We disable both the visibility ray tracer and the opacity-mask loss and optimize with PBR supervision alone. Interestingly, this baseline yields the highest NVS PSNR (and lowest LPIPS), though not the highest SSIM. We attribute this behavior to stronger appearance fitting, where albedo absorbs more illumination information and therefore reproduces the training lighting more easily. However, this entanglement hurts decomposition: albedo reconstruction and relighting quality both degrade compared to the full model.PBR-only baseline.

To isolate the visibility term, we compare the variant (with opacity-mask loss retained) against the full model. Reintroducing explicit visibility improves relighting metrics and yields cleaner shadow behavior, indicating better separation of material and illumination.Visibility.without visibility

As described in the optimization section, this term mainly acts through improved geometric support for ray-based visibility queries. Comparing with the full model shows lower relighting quality. Removing the opacity-mask loss also decreases albedo PSNR, while albedo SSIM and LPIPS remain nearly unchanged. This suggests that coarse albedo structure is preserved but radiometric consistency degrades. Better-defined occluding geometry from opacity regularization allows visibility rays to produce cleaner shadow estimates, which in turn stabilizes relighting.Opacity mask loss.without opacity loss

5

We present VisibilitySplat, an IR approach that augments 3DGS with a sparse visibility oracle for transmittance-weighted occlusion. Implemented using BVH-accelerated point-based ray tracing, the oracle complements the standard rasterized 3DGS training and visualization loop while injecting explicit visibility cues for material-illumination disentanglement. On a synthetic benchmark, we improve over several baselines in PSNR for NVS, albedo reconstruction, and relighting, while remaining competitive in SSIM and LPIPS. Ablations suggest that explicit visibility queries primarily improve relighting and decomposition quality, even when a PBR-only variant can score higher on NVS appearance metrics.

Our evaluation targets single, masked, static objects, behavior in cluttered or dynamic scenes, or under imperfect segmentation, is not assessed. The illumination model accounts for direct lighting only. Indirect transport (interreflection, subsurface, participating media) and very high-frequency environment lighting are not modeled. Finally, experiments are restricted to synthetic data, robustness to real captures, complex materials (e.g., glass, hair, translucency), and sensor noise remains untested.Limitations.

Future extensions include multi-object and full-scene evaluation, incorporation of indirect lighting, tighter coupling between splatting and visibility (e.g., differentiable or cached variants), improved geometric robustness, and investigations toward real-time deployment and comprehensive testing on real datasets.Future work.

We will release the full implementation and supporting resources upon publication of this paper.Code availability.

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

MirroS Technical Report October 8, 2026

Abstract

Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be , with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and , with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce , a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. To build the neural renderer, we adapt a pretrained video model to geometry conditions, distill it with our proposed , and optimize inference for real-time interaction. Adversarial Forcing makes history prefilling differentiable through exact replay, so that losses on later predictions update how the renderer encodes prior observations, and adds real-data adversarial supervision to improve its visual quality. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.faithfulrealisticAgentGartenneural rendererAdversarial Forcing

world models, code worlds, executable environments, neural rendering, autoregressive video generation, distribution matching distillation, agents

keywords

1

Agents learn from trajectories of actions and observations. Developing scalable, generalizable agent capabilities requires environments that not only faithfully preserve the consequences of past actions over extended interactions, but also support flexible variation in layouts, objects, and task rules. Across navigation, manipulation, and multi-agent interaction, scaling these environments therefore requires both controllable, inspectable dynamics and diverse visual observations.

However, existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off. Simulators and game engines support agent learning through explicit state and programmable interaction rules . Yet expanding their visual diversity entails substantial 3D asset creation and complex rendering pipelines, making new environments costly to build and customize. Conversely, video world models synthesize rich, interactive visual observations from data . In these models, however, task-relevant state and physical transition rules remain implicit within generated histories and learned representations, precluding direct inspection, editing, and testing of the environment’s behavior.[, , ]123[, , , ]4567

We introduce , a framework for building that combines programmable dynamics with a shared, real-time neural renderer (Figure ). In AgentGarten, each scene program runs in a simulator or game engine that maintains persistent state and executes explicit interaction rules. A shared neural renderer synthesizes the agent’s visual observations from structured conditions exported by the engine through a unified interface. This separation preserves rigorous control over state and rules while allowing compatible engines to share a single renderer. New environments can thus be authored by coding agents from text or image inputs, then edited and extended entirely in code without creating bespoke visual assets for every scene.AgentGartencode worlds1

Operating a video model as an interactive neural renderer requires it to strictly follow updated engine conditions, maintain visual consistency across extended rollouts, and synthesize observations in fine-grained, short blocks so that agents receive immediate feedback after brief actions. We adapt a pretrained bidirectional video model to structured conditions, convert it to block-causal generation, and distill it into a real-time renderer on a single GPU with , which trains the renderer on its own rollouts via distribution matching and introduces two key advances. First, to allow later losses to update the history-encoding computation without the memory cost of a fully differentiable rollout, we adopt two-pass training and introduce : a block-by-block execution schedule that eliminates numerical divergence between sampling and recomputation and achieves bitwise-identical recomputation of the rollout trajectory. Second, to prevent the visual degradation that score distillation alone exhibits over long rollouts, we incorporate a real-data adversarial objective and derive an exact R1/R2 regularization scheme for a discriminator with a frozen backbone, entirely avoiding double-backward passes through fused attention kernels.Adversarial Forcing[, , ]8910[]11exact replay[, ]1012

Code worlds provide rich environments for agents to practice and evolve. We evaluate pretrained foundation-model agents across rounds of interaction, where they perceive the world strictly through rendered observations, diagnose failures, and distill key insights into written inherited by subsequent rounds. In hide-and-seek , agents rapidly grounded abstract spatial knowledge into closed-loop physical execution, with ramp use and shelter construction emerging within a handful of games. The same reflective loop improved performance across rounds in several additional, diverse environments (Section ).playbooks[]135

Our contributions are: {contributions}

A framework for code worlds that couples persistent, editable environment state to a shared real-time neural renderer through structured conditions, enabling programmable interaction and diverse visual observations across compatible engines without per-scene visual asset authoring.

, a distillation method for a few-step, block-causal neural renderer. It combines distribution matching on self-rollouts with exact bitwise replay for history gradients, alongside a real-data adversarial objective whose exact R1/R2 regularization avoids double-backward through fused attention.Adversarial Forcing

An empirical study of evolving agents. Pretrained agents observing exclusively through neural rendering rapidly ground semantic tool knowledge and improve outcomes across rounds through written playbooks in hide-and-seek and several further distinct worlds.

2

2.1

A code world combines a scene program , an engine that executes it, and a neural renderer . The program specifies the scene and interaction rules. Let denote the scene state, including object poses, articulations, and task variables; the observing camera pose; and the actions of one or more agents. The engine updates the state and captures a structured condition from the camera:ppRθR_{\theta}sts_{t}πt\pi_{t}ata_{t}ctc_{t}

(st+1,πt+1)=fp​(st,πt,at),ct=hp​(st,πt),(s_{t+1},\pi_{t+1})=f_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t},a_{t}),\qquad c_{t}=h_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t}),(1)

where implements the state transition and renders the visible geometry. Given an appearance reference and a text description , the neural renderer generates subsequent observations from visual history :fpf_{p}hph_{p}x0x_{0}yyx<tx_{<t}

xt=Rθ​(x<t,c≤t,x0,y),t≥1.x_{t}=R_{\theta}\!\left(x_{<t},\,c_{\leq t},\,x_{0},\,y\right),\qquad t\geq 1.(2)

The agent receives and selects , which determines the next state and condition through Eq. ().xtx_{t}ata_{t}1

Unlike a video world model, whose state resides in generated history, the transition takes no rendered observation as input: the renderer influences the state only through the actions that agents select, so rendering errors cannot accumulate in the state. A recorded state trajectory can consequently be rendered again under a different appearance reference or camera without altering the underlying events. Conversely, the renderer observes the state only through ; attributes that the conditions leave undetermined, such as color and material, are specified by and and carried by the visual history. The renderer consumes conditions and visual history in blocks, as described in Section .fpf_{p}c≤tc_{\leq t}x0x_{0}yy3

2.2

We use colorized depth or surface normals as structured conditions. Both can be estimated from video or rendered by an engine, and their three-channel representation allows us to reuse the pretrained video encoder and Transformer. For real videos, we obtain depth with ViPE , using Depth Anything 3  as its depth backend, and normals with NormalCrafter . Simulated scenes supply these maps directly from geometry, without requiring detailed materials or textures. During training, each sample uses one randomly chosen modality (Section ).[]14[]15[]163.2

We encode depth with the Vision Banana mapping  and camera-space unit normals as , using consistent coordinate and orientation conventions across estimated and rendered maps (Appendix ).[]17(n+1)/2(n+1)/2A.2

2.3

A coding agent constructs a code world from either a single image or a text description, producing an executable scene program along with an appearance reference . Because appearance is delegated to the neural renderer, the scene program does not require detailed materials or leaf-level assets; it only needs coarse geometry that faithfully conveys layout, silhouettes, occlusion, and motion dynamics.x0x_{0}

From an image.

The input image serves simultaneously as and the reference layout (Figure ). Perception and generation models lift the visible content into instance masks , monocular depth and camera intrinsics , 3D bounding boxes , and extracted object meshes . A coding agent fits these assets to the estimated geometry, completes unobserved regions as plausible spatial extensions, and binds physical properties and interaction rules.x0x_{0}2[]18[]15[]19[]20

From text and agentic refinement.

When building from text, the agent writes the scene program directly using geometric primitives and engine assets. An initial render is transformed into via an image editing model while preserving scene layout. In both modalities, the agent refines the scene through an interactive feedback loop: it evaluates test rollouts from multiple probe cameras, inspects engine verification queries (contact, collision clearance, and occlusion), and iteratively repairs faulty poses, unsupported structures, or ambiguous motions before deployment.x0x_{0}

3

We train a geometry-conditioned autoregressive video model to implement the renderer in Section . Starting from a pretrained bidirectional backbone, training proceeds through geometry conditioning, teacher-forcing adaptation, and . The final stage combines distribution matching on the model’s own rollouts with exact history-gradient replay and real-data adversarial training. A bounded key–value cache and streaming decoding support continuous inference within the interaction loop in Figure .2.1Adversarial Forcing1

3.1

We initialize from Cosmos 3-Nano and separate its understanding (UND) and generation (GEN) towers. The frozen UND tower encodes the caption into per-layer keys and values consumed by GEN. This separation allows independent compilation and distributed execution of the two towers; during distillation, the student, teacher, and fake-score networks share one UND tower and reuse its outputs for the same caption.[]21yy

A frozen Wan video autoencoder maps RGB and geometry videos to latents. The appearance reference uses the backbone’s native clean-frame representation: it receives no diffusion timestep and is never denoised. Architecture sizes and training configurations are given in Appendix .[]22x0x_{0}A.1

3.2

Condition tokens.

Depth and normals use the three-channel encodings of Section . Spatial average pooling reduces the condition encoder’s input size and the number of tokens processed during training and inference. For an encoded condition frame indexed by , we form2.2tt

where pools the condition video spatially, is the frozen video encoder, and groups latent patches. We reuse the pretrained RGB input projection and add a zero-initialized modality embedding . Condition tokens receive no diffusion timestep.SSEE𝒫\mathcal{P}WinW_{\mathrm{in}}egeoe_{\mathrm{geo}}

Joint attention.

We concatenate geometry and RGB tokens along the sequence dimension and process them with the same Transformer layers. We use neither channel concatenation nor control branches , to avoid imposing a pixel-aligned inductive bias. Writing for RGB latent tokens, the visual sequence is[]23[, ]2425RtR_{t}

[G0,G1,…]​[R0,R1,…],[\,G_{0},G_{1},\dots\,]\;[\,R_{0},R_{1},\dots\,],(4)

with encoding and text keys and values integrated via cross-attention. Geometry and RGB share temporal rotary coordinates; spatial coordinates map both grids to the same image extent. This preserves geometric alignment while allowing cross-token interactions. Only noisy RGB tokens produce velocity predictions.R0R_{0}x0x_{0}

Robust conditions.

Geometry estimated from natural video differs from engine-rendered geometry in texture leakage, alignment, and missing observations. To reduce dependence on estimator-specific cues, we randomly retain depth or normals, with occasional dropout of both modalities; dropped inputs are black. We suppress fine texture by down- and upsampling, perturb alignment with a smooth spatial warp anchored to the first frame, and add noise to condition latents. Preprocessing and augmentation settings appear in Appendix .A.2

3.3

Stage 2 adapts the geometry-conditioned model to blockwise autoregressive generation. We partition the latents after the reference into fixed-length blocks. Each block is generated from its aligned geometry and previously completed blocks, without access to future blocks.

Parallel teacher forcing.

Training uses two copies of each block inside one Transformer: a clean copy that represents history and a noisy copy that is denoised. Each copy carries its own aligned condition tokens. With the reference, the attention mask permitsPjP_{j}QjQ_{j}A0A_{0}

The noisy copy of a block therefore sees clean earlier blocks and attends bidirectionally within itself, but never its own clean target. This lets all target blocks be trained in parallel with independently sampled flow times. 3.4

Stage 3, , distills the teacher-forced model into a few-step renderer that is trained on its own rollouts. It has three components: distribution matching against the bidirectional teacher, exact replay of each rollout so that gradients reach the history it wrote, and a real-data adversarial objective with exact R1/R2 regularization.Adversarial Forcing

3.4.1

We match autoregressive student rollouts to the bidirectional teacher through distribution matching distillation (DMD) in the manner of Self Forcing . The student starts from stage 2 and generates each block in a few denoising steps, conditioning on its own preceding outputs. The frozen stage-1 teacher scores the resulting clip jointly. An auxiliary model, initialized from the teacher, learns the student’s distribution.[, , ]8910fake-score

For a student prediction corrupted to , let and denote clean estimates from the teacher and fake-score model. The student objective isz~θ\widetilde{z}_{\theta}yτ=(1−τ)​z~θ+τ​ϵy_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\widetilde{z}_{\theta}+\tau\epsilonfTf_{\mathrm{T}}fψf_{\psi}

where is a per-video normalization, the number of latent elements, and stops gradients. The fake-score model is trained by flow matching on detached student samples. Sampling schedules, guidance, and update ratios are specified in Appendix .aaNNsg\operatorname{sg}A.4

The other two components extend this objective: replay restores gradients through history encoding, and an adversarial loss supplies supervision from real videos.

3.4.2

In standard Self Forcing, completed blocks are encoded into a detached KV cache. Subsequent losses therefore supervise prediction from that cache, but not the history-prefill computation that produced its keys and values. Keeping this computation differentiable in a single serial rollout would retain the recursively connected cache-formation graphs across blocks, with substantial memory cost.

Similar to Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) , we decouple rollout and gradient propagation using two passes. A no-gradient rollout records each block’s input at the final denoising time and its clean output . A differentiable replay then recomputes both history and predictions with the visibility pattern of Eq. (). For block ,[]11UUt∗t^{*}ZZ5jj

z~θ,j=sg(Uj)−t∗vθ(sg(Uj),t∗∣sg(Z<j),𝒞;ℳTF).\widetilde{z}_{\theta,j}=\operatorname{sg}(U_{j})-t^{*}\,v_{\theta}\!\left(\operatorname{sg}(U_{j}),t^{*}\mid\operatorname{sg}(Z_{<j}),\mathcal{C};\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{TF}}\right).(8)

The recorded latents stay detached, but their history encodings are recomputed inside the graph. Later losses thus update the parameters that write history into the cache, without differentiating through the sampling trajectory. Both DMD and generator adversarial losses use this replayed prediction.

SGF implements its second pass with full-sequence FlexAttention . Although the attention mask matches cached generation, the kernel, tensor shapes, and reduction order differ; in finite precision, replay can consequently diverge from the sampled trajectory. We preserve the rollout’s execution structure: attention runs block by block with scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), using the same key–value order and call shapes. Projections and feed-forward layers use the same block grouping as well. The history keys and values are recomputed and assembled differentiably, so the matching execution retains the history-gradient path (Figure ). Section  evaluates numerical agreement and cost.[]2644.2

3.4.3

Distribution matching uses teacher and fake-score estimates on generated samples, without directly contrasting them with real videos. Following DMD2 , we add an adversarial objective. A trainable head aggregates intermediate features from the frozen teacher backbone into a discriminator logit. Conditioning the backbone on geometry and the reference lets the discriminator assess appearance together with geometric consistency. Section  compares the resulting renderer with one trained by Self Forcing alone.[]10hϕh_{\phi}BB4.1

We use the relativistic pairing of R3GAN . With and the logits of a real clip and of the student’s prediction, corrupted with the same noise and timestep under the same conditions,[]12rrff

3.5

The renderer prefills the reference and text, denoises incoming blocks, and commits clean predictions into a bounded KV cache. The cache maintains a permanent prefix (including ) and a sliding window of recent history (Figure ). For rollouts exceeding the training horizon, we apply top-aligned rotary position remapping: the active block is clamped at the horizon boundary while recent history is shifted to precede it and re-rotated, preserving relative temporal distances while geometry tracks the true simulation timeline (Appendix ).sinkx0x_{0}6C

Low-latency execution and deployment.

Transformer execution over short blocks is primarily bounded by memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead. Rather than relying on , which incurs minutes-long cold-start compilation delays, we implement custom Triton kernels to fuse elementwise operations around attention (RMSNorm, RoPE rotation, and gated activations) without intermediate memory round-trips. CUDA graph capture and replay further eliminate host-side launch overhead for fixed-shape blocks. To bypass the heavy latent decoding bottleneck during real-time serving, we optionally replace the standard VAE decoder with a distilled tiny decoder , which reconstructs pixel frames in under 10 ms (Table ). In interactive deployments, the engine pushes conditions to a GPU worker, and decoded frames are streamed to the agent or browser over WebRTC with bounded queuing latency (Section ).torch.compile[]29[]30[]3124.3

4

We examine visual quality in long rollouts, replay accuracy, and inference throughput. Performance measurements use one NVIDIA H100 GPU, BF16 computation, output, blocks of four latent frames, and the four-step sampler unless stated otherwise.480×832480\times 832

4.1

Figure  compares 30-second rollouts from renderers trained with Self Forcing and with Adversarial Forcing on the same condition trajectories. With Self Forcing, rollouts develop repetitive surface patterns and lose scene detail as they grow longer. Adversarial Forcing retains natural textures and fine detail throughout.7

4.2

Table  measures recomputation error and cost with only the attention execution changed. Full-sequence FlexAttention replay differs from the cached rollout by 3.99% relative error; block-by-block SDPA replay is bitwise identical. Forward time decreases by 5.4%, while total peak memory changes by 0.2%.1L2L_{2}

4.3

With the hand-written kernels, CUDA graph capture, and the tiny decoder (Section ), the renderer generates video at over 35 frames per second on one NVIDIA H100 GPU, including condition encoding, four denoising steps, decoding, and host transfer. Table  breaks one served block of sixteen frames into its parts. The cache keeps five sink and 44 recent latent frames, one of the history windows used in distillation (Appendix ), so each four-frame block attends to 49 frames of history. The block is measured at steady state with the cache full: blocks 17 to 48 of a 48-block, 769-frame rollout, averaged over two rollouts. Attention is dense and the tiny decoder runs in FP16.3.5480×832480\times 8322C

5

Code worlds give agents many places to act, and a world that answers every action is also a place to practice. This section presents environments built on the shared renderer, revisits hide-and-seek with agents that perceive the world only through rendered observations, describes the round-by-round procedure through which they improve, and applies it to four further worlds.

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

MirroS Technical Report October 8, 2026

Abstract

Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be , with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and , with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce , a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.faithfulrealisticAgentGartenneural rendererAdversarial Forcing

world models, code worlds, executable environments, neural rendering, autoregressive video generation, distribution matching distillation, agents

keywords

1

Agents learn from trajectories of actions and observations. Developing scalable, generalizable agent capabilities requires environments that not only faithfully preserve the consequences of past actions over extended interactions, but also support flexible variation in layouts, objects, and task rules. Across navigation, manipulation, and multi-agent interaction, scaling these environments therefore requires both controllable, inspectable dynamics and diverse visual observations.

However, existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off. Simulators and game engines support agent learning through explicit state and programmable interaction rules . Yet expanding their visual diversity entails substantial 3D asset creation and complex rendering pipelines, making new environments costly to build and customize. Conversely, video world models synthesize rich, interactive visual observations from data . In these models, however, task-relevant state and physical transition rules remain implicit within generated histories and learned representations, precluding direct inspection, editing, and testing of the environment’s behavior.[, , ]123[, , , ]4567

We introduce , a framework for building that combines programmable dynamics with a shared, real-time neural renderer (Figure ). In AgentGarten, each scene program runs in a simulator or game engine that maintains persistent state and executes explicit interaction rules. A shared neural renderer synthesizes the agent’s visual observations from structured conditions exported by the engine through a unified interface. This separation preserves rigorous control over state and rules while allowing compatible engines to share a single renderer. New environments can thus be authored by coding agents from text or image inputs, then edited and extended entirely in code without creating bespoke visual assets for every scene.AgentGartencode worlds1

Operating a video model as an interactive neural renderer requires it to strictly follow updated engine conditions, maintain visual consistency across extended rollouts, and synthesize observations in fine-grained, short blocks so that agents receive immediate feedback after brief actions. We adapt a pretrained bidirectional video model to structured conditions, convert it to block-causal generation, and distill it into a real-time renderer on a single GPU with , which trains the renderer on its own rollouts via distribution matching and introduces two key advances. First, to allow later losses to update the history-encoding computation without the memory cost of a fully differentiable rollout, we adopt two-pass training and introduce : a block-by-block execution schedule that eliminates numerical divergence between sampling and recomputation and achieves bitwise-identical recomputation of the rollout trajectory. Second, to prevent the visual degradation that score distillation alone exhibits over long rollouts, we incorporate a real-data adversarial objective and derive an exact R1/R2 regularization scheme for a discriminator with a frozen backbone, entirely avoiding double-backward passes through fused attention kernels.Adversarial Forcing[, , ]8910[]11exact replay[, ]1012

Code worlds provide rich environments for agents to practice and evolve. We evaluate pretrained foundation-model agents across rounds of interaction, where they perceive the world strictly through rendered observations, diagnose failures, and distill key insights into written inherited by subsequent rounds. In hide-and-seek , agents rapidly grounded abstract spatial knowledge into closed-loop physical execution, with ramp use and shelter construction emerging within a handful of games. The same reflective loop improved performance across rounds in several additional, diverse environments (Section ).playbooks[]135

Our contributions are: {contributions}

A framework for code worlds that couples persistent, editable environment state to a shared real-time neural renderer through structured conditions, enabling programmable interaction and diverse visual observations across compatible engines without per-scene visual asset authoring.

, a distillation method for a few-step, block-causal neural renderer. It combines distribution matching on self-rollouts with exact bitwise replay for history gradients, alongside a real-data adversarial objective whose exact R1/R2 regularization avoids double-backward through fused attention.Adversarial Forcing

An empirical study of evolving agents. Pretrained agents observing exclusively through neural rendering rapidly ground semantic tool knowledge and improve outcomes across rounds through written playbooks in hide-and-seek and several further distinct worlds.

2

2.1

Let denote the scene state, including object poses, articulations, and task variables; the observing camera pose; and the actions of one or more agents. where implements the state transition and renders the visible geometry. Given an appearance reference and a text description , the neural renderer generates subsequent observations from visual history :fpf_{p}hph_{p}x0x_{0}yyx<tx_{<t}

A recorded state trajectory can consequently be rendered again under a different appearance reference or camera without altering the underlying events. Conversely, the renderer observes the state only through ; attributes that the conditions leave undetermined, such as color and material, are specified by and and carried by the visual history. 2.2

We use colorized depth or surface normals as structured conditions. Both can be estimated from video or rendered by an engine, and their three-channel representation allows us to reuse the pretrained video encoder and Transformer. For real videos, we obtain depth with ViPE , using Depth Anything 3  as its depth backend, and normals with NormalCrafter . Simulated scenes supply these maps directly from geometry, without requiring detailed materials or textures. During training, each sample uses one randomly chosen modality (Section ).[]14[]15[]163.2

We encode depth with the Vision Banana mapping  and camera-space unit normals as , using consistent coordinate and orientation conventions across estimated and rendered maps (Appendix ).[]17(n+1)/2(n+1)/2A.2

2.3

A coding agent constructs a code world from either a single image or a text description, producing an executable scene program along with an appearance reference . Because appearance is delegated to the neural renderer, the scene program does not require detailed materials or leaf-level assets; it only needs coarse geometry that faithfully conveys layout, silhouettes, occlusion, and motion dynamics.x0x_{0}

From an image.

The input image serves simultaneously as and the reference layout (Figure ). Perception and generation models lift the visible content into instance masks , monocular depth and camera intrinsics , 3D bounding boxes , and extracted object meshes . A coding agent fits these assets to the estimated geometry, completes unobserved regions as plausible spatial extensions, and binds physical properties and interaction rules.x0x_{0}2[]18[]15[]19[]20

From text and agentic refinement.

When building from text, the agent writes the scene program directly using geometric primitives and engine assets. An initial render is transformed into via an image editing model while preserving scene layout. In both modalities, the agent refines the scene through an interactive feedback loop: it evaluates test rollouts from multiple probe cameras, inspects engine verification queries (contact, collision clearance, and occlusion), and iteratively repairs faulty poses, unsupported structures, or ambiguous motions before deployment.x0x_{0}

We train a geometry-conditioned autoregressive video model to implement the renderer in Section . Starting from a pretrained bidirectional backbone, training proceeds through geometry conditioning, teacher-forcing adaptation, and . The final stage combines distribution matching on the model’s own rollouts with exact history-gradient replay and real-data adversarial training. A bounded key–value cache and streaming decoding support continuous inference within the interaction loop in Figure .2.1Adversarial Forcing1

Geometry estimated from natural video differs from engine-rendered geometry in texture leakage, alignment, and missing observations. The renderer prefills the reference and text, denoises incoming blocks, and commits clean predictions into a bounded KV cache. The cache maintains a permanent prefix (including ) and a sliding window of recent history (Figure ). For rollouts exceeding the training horizon, we apply top-aligned rotary position remapping: the active block is clamped at the horizon boundary while recent history is shifted to precede it and re-rotated, preserving relative temporal distances while geometry tracks the true simulation timeline (Appendix ).sinkx0x_{0}6C

Low-latency execution and deployment.

Transformer execution over short blocks is primarily bounded by memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead. Rather than relying on , which incurs minutes-long cold-start compilation delays, we implement custom Triton kernels to fuse elementwise operations around attention (RMSNorm, RoPE rotation, and gated activations) without intermediate memory round-trips. CUDA graph capture and replay further eliminate host-side launch overhead for fixed-shape blocks. To bypass the heavy latent decoding bottleneck during real-time serving, we optionally replace the standard VAE decoder with a distilled tiny decoder , which reconstructs pixel frames in under 10 ms (Table ). In interactive deployments, the engine pushes conditions to a GPU worker, and decoded frames are streamed to the agent or browser over WebRTC with bounded queuing latency (Section ).torch.compile[]29[]30[]3124.3

5

Code worlds give agents many places to act, and a world that answers every action is also a place to practice. This section presents environments built on the shared renderer, revisits hide-and-seek with agents that perceive the world only through rendered observations, describes the round-by-round procedure through which they improve, and applies it to four further worlds.
